claim: GAO's contracting snapshots state that other transaction agreement data are not included in federal contract obligations. They report OTA spending separately, at $16.5 billion in FY2020, nearly $16 billion in FY2023, $18.4 billion in FY2024 and $18.2 billion in FY2025.
numbers: FY2020 $16.5 billion (GAO-BLOG-SNAPSHOT-FY2020). FY2023 nearly $16 billion (GAO-DASHBOARD-CURRENT-DATA). FY2024 $18.4 billion in constant FY2024 dollars (GAO-DASHBOARD-FY2024-DATA). FY2025 $18.2 billion, a $700 million decrease from FY2024 in constant FY2025 dollars (this source). Each snapshot uses its own dollar year.
quote: Data on other transaction agreements are not included in data on federal contract obligations.
our_interpretation: GAO treats OTAs as outside contract totals, which supports treating them as outside our File D1 universe and as a scope gap of roughly $16 billion to $18 billion a year in recent years.

claim: DoD obligations through prototype and production OTAs grew from $1.8 billion in FY2016 to over $18 billion in FY2024. From FY2021 to FY2024 DoD obligated $62.9 billion on OTAs, and 10 vendors received about 57 percent of it.
numbers: $1.8 billion (FY2016) to over $18 billion (FY2024). $62.9 billion FY2021 to FY2024. 10 vendors $35.9 billion (about 57 percent). Prototype OTAs over $16 billion in FY2024. Production OTAs $2 billion in FY2024.
quote: DOD obligations through OTAs for prototyping and production have significantly increased, growing from $1.8 billion in fiscal year 2016 to over $18 billion in fiscal year 2024.
our_interpretation: OTA spending outside FAR contract data grew about tenfold over our window, so DoD research and prototype cells understate the real market more in FY2019 to FY2025 than in FY2008 to FY2015.
test_idea: Track DoD dollars in R&D PSC cells (A codes) by FY and compare the trend with these OTA totals to check whether FAR contract dollars dip as OTA use rises.

claim: GAO found that over $40 billion in other transaction agreements (OTAs) appeared on an agency website or in the FPDS OTA Module but were not reported to USAspending.gov. More than $10 billion appeared COVID-19 related. The data covered FY2020 to FY2022.
numbers: Over $40 billion not on USAspending.gov, more than $10 billion COVID-19 related. Figure 2 (image) shows the FPDS OTA Module part as three agencies with over $40 billion in OTA awards and the website part as one agency with almost $700 million. OTA obligations government-wide grew from $4.8 billion (2018) to $11 billion (FY2022), peaking at $18.4 billion in FY2020.
period_covered: FY2020 to FY2022, data obtained December 2022 to June 2023
agencies: Three agencies via FPDS OTA Module, one via its website (names not given in text)
quote: For example, over $40 billion in OTAs were either reported on an agency’s website or the Federal Procurement Data System (FPDS) OTA Module—a government data system for agencies to report certain OTAs and associated obligations.
our_interpretation: OTA spending sits outside File D1, so R&D and prototype markets where OTAs substitute for contracts look smaller and possibly more concentrated in our cells, mostly for FY2020 to FY2022.
test_idea: awarding_agency_code, product_or_service_code (R&D codes), award_description: check for rows describing other transactions and track DoD and HHS R&D cell totals FY2018 to FY2025.

claim: FPDS holds DoD prototype and production OTAs in a separate OTA module. DoD does not report research OTAs to FPDS at all because they count as assistance instruments.
quote: It also includes a module for reporting certain OTAs. DOD reports its use of prototype and production OTAs in the OTA module of FPDS. DOD does not report research OTAs in FPDS because they are considered assistance instruments.
our_interpretation: OTA dollars sit outside the FAR contract records that feed our File D1 cells, so DoD research and prototype buying through consortia is missing from our HHI and CR4 unless the archive carries OTA module rows, which we have not confirmed.
test_idea: Look for OTA records in the archive (award or IDV type codes for other transactions, or OTA text in transaction_description) by FY and report dollars found.

claim: GAO reported that USAspending.gov has no identifier for OTAs. OMB told agencies to report OTAs by the funding type they resemble, while Treasury said OTAs are not federal awards under FFATA and should not be reported.
quote: Because USAspending.gov does not contain an identifier for OTAs, there is not a systematic way to identify OTAs on USAspending.gov.
our_interpretation: OTAs that agencies did report could sit in contract data without a flag, so a few rows in our data may be OTAs that we cannot isolate.
test_idea: award_description, type_of_contract_pricing, award_type: count rows with 'OTHER TRANSACTION' or 'OTA' in the description by agency and year.

claim: FAR 4.606(c)(6) bars reporting of contract actions whose required data would be classified. The 2011 proposed rule said FPDS is not approved to hold classified data and the FAR had not said so expressly.
period_covered: Explicit in the FAR from 2012-12-20 (FAC 2005-62). Practice predates it per the 2011 preamble.
quote: Classified actions are not reported to FPDS, since FPDS is not approved to handle classified information, but this is not expressly stated in the FAR
our_interpretation: Classified contract dollars are missing in every year of our window, which most affects DoD and intelligence-related cells.

claim: FAR 4.606(c)(5) bars reporting of actions that other authority keeps out of FPDS, with national security as the example.
period_covered: Current FAR. Present before the December 2012 rule, which added (c)(6) to (c)(11).
quote: Actions that, pursuant to other authority, will not be entered in FPDS ( e.g. , reporting of the information would compromise national security).
our_interpretation: Some defense and intelligence buying is absent with no marker, so cells in those PSCs can look more concentrated or smaller than they are.

claim: DoD also bars reporting of contracts, agreements or orders that are themselves classified.
quote: Contracts, agreements, or orders that are themselves classified.
our_interpretation: Classified DoD contracts are absent from our data entirely.

claim: FAR 4.603(b) and 4.606(a)(1) set the floor for FPDS reporting. Agencies must report unclassified contract actions above the micro-purchase threshold, plus any modification that changes reported data at any dollar value.
numbers: Floor is the micro-purchase threshold (MPT) in force on the action date.
period_covered: Current FAR (FAC 2026-01). Same structure since FAC 2005-25 (2008-04-22).
quote: Executive agencies shall use FPDS to maintain publicly available information about all unclassified contract actions exceeding the micro-purchase threshold , and any modifications to those actions that change previously reported contract action report data, regardless of dollar value.
our_interpretation: Base awards at or below the MPT are mostly outside our data, so HHI and CR4 describe the above-threshold market only.
test_idea: Columns fiscal_year, awarding_agency_code, federal_action_obligation, award_type_code. Count rows with absolute obligation at or below the micro-purchase threshold in force that year, by agency and FY.

claim: The FPDS welcome text lists what FPDS does not hold. The list includes purchase card data, data from agencies not subject to FAR reporting rules, interagency agreements, imprest fund transactions and actions paid only with non-appropriated funds.
numbers: none
pinpoint: FPDS welcome text, section "What's not in FPDS-NG?"
quote: Data from agencies not subject to FPDS reporting requirements according to the Federal Acquisition Regulations
our_interpretation: Purchase card buys and non-FAR agencies are outside our data entirely, so their vendors never enter any HHI or CR4 cell.

claim: FAR 4.606(c)(1) bars reporting of imprest fund transactions below the micro-purchase threshold, including purchase card buys, unless an agency's own procedures call for reporting them.
period_covered: Current FAR. Same wording in the 2008 interim rule.
quote: Imprest fund transactions below the micro-purchase threshold , including those made via the Government purchase card (unless specific agency procedures prescribe reporting these actions).
our_interpretation: Open-market purchase card spending below the MPT is outside our data, and agency procedures can pull some of it in.
test_idea: Columns purchase_card_as_payment_method_code, federal_action_obligation, awarding_agency_code, fiscal_year. Share of rows paid by card and below the MPT, by agency and FY.

claim: DoD tells offices not to report open-market purchase card buys below the micro-purchase threshold.
period_covered: Current PGI. Same rule since the 2011-09-20 revision.
quote: Do not report open-market purchases (i.e., not under a Federal Supply schedule, agreement, or contract) made with the GPC valued less than the micro-purchase threshold to FPDS.
our_interpretation: DoD open-market card buying below the MPT is outside our data.

claim: FPDS covers appropriated funds only. FAR 4.603(d) says mixed-funded actions report only the appropriated part, and 4.606(b)(2) makes non-appropriated fund actions optional with approval.
period_covered: Current FAR. Mixed funding rule since FAC 2005-25 (2008). Approval wording since 2012-12-20.
quote: Agencies awarding contract actions with a mix of appropriated and non-appropriated funding shall only report the full appropriated portion of the contract action in FPDS.
our_interpretation: Non-appropriated fund buying (for example by exchange services) is outside our data, and mixed contracts show only part of their value.

claim: The FAR definition of a contract action excludes grants, cooperative agreements, other transactions, real property leases, requisitions from Federal stock, training authorizations and other non-FAR transactions.
period_covered: Current FAR. Same definition in the 2008 interim rule.
quote: Contract action does not include grants, cooperative agreements, other transactions, real property leases, requisitions from Federal stock, training authorizations, or other non-FAR based transactions.
our_interpretation: Other transactions sit outside the FAR reporting duty, so any OT rows in our file come from separate agency practice and may not be complete.
test_idea: Columns type_of_contract_pricing, award_type_code, idv_type_code, fiscal_year. Count rows and dollars coded as other transaction, by agency and FY.

claim: GAO defined contract obligations in FPDS-NG as obligations on FAR-based contracts. They exclude grants, cooperative agreements, loans, other transactions for research, real property leases and requisitions from federal stock.
quote: "contract obligations" means obligations on contracts that are subject to the Federal Acquisition Regulation, and does not include, for example, grants, cooperative agreements, loans, other transactions for research, real property leases, or requisitions from federal stock.
our_interpretation: Our cells cover FAR contract buying only, so markets where agencies also buy through leases, stock requisitions or OTAs are only partly measured.

claim: DOE may count small business subcontracts toward its small business prime contracting goal, starting in 2014. NNSA prime contracts reach FPDS through DOE's procurement system, while M&O subcontracts are reported in MOSRC and eSRS instead.
numbers: Authority from the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2014. MOSRC holds only about 50 percent of M&O small business contracts because sensitive and classified awards are left out.
quote: Since 2014, DOE has been allowed, in addition to considering prime contracts in meeting small business goals, to count subcontracts with small businesses to help achieve its small business prime contracting goal.
our_interpretation: DOE spending through M&O contracts shows up in our data as a few very large prime awards to the M&O operators, so DOE cells look highly concentrated even though the operators buy from many subcontractors we cannot observe.
test_idea: For DOE cells, report the share of dollars going to the top M&O operators by PSC (operation of government-owned facility codes) and FY.

claim: GAO noted that the FAR does not apply to all executive branch agencies. It generally does not cover acquisitions funded with nonappropriated funds, and some agencies, such as the FAA, have authority to use other acquisition systems.
agencies: FAA and agencies using nonappropriated funds
quote: For example, it generally does not apply to acquisitions that are funded with nonappropriated funds, and some agencies and programs may have statutory authority to use other acquisition systems, such as the Federal Aviation Administration.
our_interpretation: Buying outside the FAR need not reach FPDS, so whole agencies or programs can be partly or fully absent from our cells.
test_idea: awarding_agency_code and awarding_sub_agency_code (FAA): FAA obligations by fiscal year compared with DOT totals to check whether FAA contracting is present.

claim: FAR 4.606(c)(2) bars reporting of orders from GSA stock and the GSA Global Supply Program.
period_covered: Current FAR. Same wording in the 2008 interim rule.
quote: Orders from GSA stock and the GSA Global Supply Program.
our_interpretation: Agency buys from GSA stock never appear as agency rows, so cells for common supply PSCs miss that demand.

claim: FAR 4.606(c)(3) bars reporting of purchases at GSA or AbilityOne service stores, because GSA already reported the stocked items.
period_covered: Current FAR. The 2008 interim rule used the older JWOD name.
quote: Purchases made at GSA or AbilityOne service stores, as these items stocked for resale have already been reported by GSA.
our_interpretation: Store purchases are counted once under GSA's own buying, so the buying agency cells look smaller than real demand.

claim: FAR 4.606(c)(7) to (c)(9) bar reporting of resale (commissary or exchange), revenue generating concessions, and training expenditures not issued as orders or contracts.
period_covered: Current FAR. These were optional with notice to the FPDS Program Office from 2008-04-22 to 2012-12-19.
quote: Resale activity (i.e., commissary or exchange activity).
our_interpretation: Commissary resale buying is outside our data, which matters for DoD food and consumer PSC cells.

claim: FAR 4.606(c)(10) bars reporting of interagency agreements other than the interagency acquisitions that 4.606(a)(1) requires.
period_covered: Current FAR. Optional with notice before 2012-12-20.
quote: Interagency agreements other than inter-agency acquisitions required to be reported at 4.606 (a)(1).
our_interpretation: Work one agency buys from another agency directly is not in our data, while assisted acquisitions that end in a contract are.

claim: FAR 4.606(c)(4) bars reporting of purchases with non-appropriated fund activity cards, chaplain fund cards, individual training orders and Defense Printing orders.
period_covered: Current FAR. Same list in the 2008 interim rule.
quote: Purchases made using non-appropriated fund activity cards, chaplain fund cards, individual Government personnel training orders, and Defense Printing orders.
our_interpretation: These channels are outside our data and are small dollar.

claim: USAspending says agencies must report contract awards above the micro-purchase threshold to FPDS under FAR 4.606. It gives the threshold as $10,000 as of 2022, with a few exceptions.
numbers: $10,000 micro-purchase threshold as of 2022
pinpoint: About the Data, "Reporting Threshold for Prime Awards", paragraph 2
quote: Additionally, Federal agencies must report all contract and financial assistance awards that are above a micro-purchase threshold to the
our_interpretation: Contract actions at or below the threshold are outside the reporting duty, so small purchases are only partly in our data and their share depends on agency practice.
test_idea: base_and_all_options_value, federal_action_obligation, action_date. Share of rows and dollars at or below the threshold in force each year, by awarding agency and FY.

claim: USAspending lists sub-threshold awards as one cause of unlinked awards. An agency may report a micro-purchase in File C but not in File D1, or the reverse.
numbers: none
pinpoint: About the Data, "Limited Data for Unlinked Prime Awards", list of other causes, item 3
quote: The award is under the micropurchase threshold, and the agency reports it in File C but not File D1/D2, or vice versa.
our_interpretation: Micro-purchases that an agency books only in its financial system (File C) never reach FPDS, so they are absent from our File D1 based cells.

claim: GSA describes the contract award data now searched in SAM.gov as all unclassified contract actions above the micro-purchase threshold, plus modifications that change reported data at any dollar value.
numbers: none
quote: Search results contain publicly available information about all unclassified contract actions exceeding the micro-purchase threshold and any modifications to those actions that change previously reported data, regardless of dollar value.
our_interpretation: Classified contract actions are outside the public data by design, which removes some intelligence and defense vendors from our cells.

claim: FFATA required contracts above $25,000 on USASpending.gov, while FPDS-NG held contracts above the micro-purchase threshold, then $3,000. GAO also said no authoritative source lists all contracts each agency issues.
numbers: FFATA threshold $25,000. FPDS-NG threshold above the $3,000 micro-purchase threshold (2014 report).
period_covered: FY2012 (rule in force at the time)
pinpoint: p. 4, footnote 5 (PDF p. 8), and p. 11, footnote 26 (PDF p. 15)
quote: Although FFATA requires reporting of contracts above $25,000 to USASpending.gov, FPDS-NG contains data on contracts valued above the micro-purchase threshold of $3,000.
our_interpretation: Purchases at or below the micro-purchase threshold are largely missing by design, which mostly removes small actions and few dollars from each cell.
test_idea: federal_action_obligation, action_date_fiscal_year: share of rows and of dollars with absolute value at or below 3,000, 3,500 and 10,000 by year.

claim: Actions at or below the micro-purchase threshold are optional. FAR 4.606(b)(1) lets an agency report them only if they can be kept apart from FAR-based actions and the FPDS Program Office approves in writing.
period_covered: Current FAR. Written approval and segregation wording dates from FAC 2005-62 (effective 2012-12-20).
quote: Agencies may submit actions other than those listed at paragraph (a)(1) of this section only if they are able to be segregated from FAR-based actions and this is approved in writing by the FPDS Program Office.
our_interpretation: Small optional actions can enter the data for some agencies and years only, which changes action counts far more than dollars.
test_idea: Columns fiscal_year, awarding_agency_code, federal_action_obligation, award_type_code. Count rows with absolute obligation at or below the micro-purchase threshold in force that year, by agency and FY.

claim: DoD encourages, but does not require, reports for purchase orders under micro-purchase procedures below the threshold that were not paid by purchase card or Standard Form 44.
numbers: Contingency awards must be reported above $25,000.
period_covered: Current PGI. Same text in the 2014 revision.
quote: Although a contract action report is not required for these awards when micro-purchase procedures were followed and the value is less than the MPT, it is encouraged as a best practice if the award was not accomplished using the Governmentwide commercial purchase card (GPC) or a Standard Form 44.
our_interpretation: DoD offices differ in how many small purchase orders they report, so small-row counts are not comparable across offices.
test_idea: Columns awarding_office_code, award_type_code (purchase order), federal_action_obligation, fiscal_year. Share of purchase orders below the MPT by DoD office and FY.

claim: DoD adds its own exclusions. Ordering officers do not report orders under USTRANSCOM transportation vehicles or DLA Energy vehicles because those commands report them in consolidated form.
numbers: Consolidated reports to USTRANSCOM at least annually.
quote: USTRANSCOM will report these orders. Contracting officers shall submit consolidated reports of orders (bookings/bills of lading) at least annually to USTRANSCOM
our_interpretation: Many transport orders collapse into few consolidated rows under one reporting office, which cuts action counts and may shift the recorded office.
test_idea: Columns awarding_sub_agency_code, awarding_office_code, number_of_actions, product_or_service_code (V series). Compare rows with number_of_actions above 1 for USTRANSCOM offices by FY.

claim: FAR 4.606(a)(2) says GSA's charge card office will give purchase card data to FPDS at least yearly for reports. The text does not say these data become contract action rows.
numbers: At a minimum annually.
period_covered: Current FAR. Paragraph (a)(3) in the 2008 interim rule.
quote: The GSA Office of Charge Card Management will provide the Government purchase card data, at a minimum annually, and GSA will incorporate that data into FPDS for reports.
our_interpretation: We do not know whether this card data reaches File D1, so we treat open-market card spending as outside our data.

claim: GAO counted OTA use for FY2010 to FY2014 from each agency's own systems and documents. It noted that agencies use various data systems to track OTAs. Eleven federal agencies hold OTA authority.
numbers: 11 agencies with OTA authority. Period FY2010 to FY2014.
agencies: NASA, DoD, DOE, HHS, DHS, DOT and five component agencies
quote: Agencies use various data systems to track and record their use of other transaction agreements.
our_interpretation: OTA spending before FY2016 is not reliably in FPDS, so it sits outside our FY2008 to FY2015 cells and cannot be added back from contract data.

claim: SBA's small business goaling report leaves out certain contract dollars when computing small business shares, mainly contracts not subject to the FAR. SBA put the FY2011 base after these exclusions at $423 billion.
numbers: $423 billion goaling base in FY2011
quote: In its annual report on small business procurement goals, SBA excludes certain contract dollars when calculating percentages of dollars obligated to small businesses.
our_interpretation: Small business shares built from our full File D1 universe will not match SBA scorecard figures, because SBA uses a narrower base.

claim: FAR 4.606(c)(11) bars reporting of letters of obligation used in the A-76 process.
period_covered: Current FAR. Optional with notice before 2012-12-20.
quote: Letters of obligation used in the A-76 process.
our_interpretation: A-76 letters of obligation go to in-house providers and do not name a vendor, so they do not touch vendor shares.

claim: GAO reported that the Treasury broker pulled FPDS-NG data by awarding agency rather than funding agency, so some agencies' procurement data appeared in their shared service provider's File D1. Agencies said Treasury fixed this starting Q1 FY2019.
numbers: Fix reported from FY2019 Q1.
agencies: Agencies served by shared service providers
quote: the Treasury broker was designed to pull data from FPDS-NG based on the awarding agency instead of the funding agency.
our_interpretation: Our cells use the awarding agency code, so contracts awarded by a provider for a client agency count in the provider's cells in every year, regardless of the broker fix.
test_idea: awarding_agency_code, funding_agency_code: cross-tabulate awarding by funding agency for FY2018 and FY2019 to check whether attribution shifts at the fix.

claim: For Q4 FY2018, 34 non-CFO Act agencies submitted an empty File D1. Agencies said their procurement went into a shared service provider's file, their awards were below the micro-purchase threshold, or they did not use FPDS-NG.
numbers: 34 non-CFO Act agencies with blank File D1, 16 of which also had a blank File C. 96 agencies submitted.
quote: Specifically, 34 non-CFO Act agencies submitted a blank File D1, which contains procurement data, and 16 of those 34 also submitted a blank File C.
our_interpretation: Some small agencies buy through a shared service provider, so their contracts can sit under the provider's awarding agency code in our cells.
test_idea: awarding_agency_code, funding_agency_code, federal_action_obligation: share of each agency's funded dollars that another agency awarded, by fiscal year.

claim: In FY2012, 33 of 37 agencies with budget authority of at least $400 million showed at least one contract on USASpending.gov. FDIC, NCUA and TVA said their contracts use non-appropriated funds and are exempt. The CIA did not report contracts at all.
numbers: 33 of 37 agencies reported at least one contract. The 4 that did not were FDIC, NCUA and TVA (non-appropriated funds claim) and CIA (classified and unclassified contracts withheld).
pinpoint: p. 12 (PDF p. 16), with footnote 27 on p. 11 (PDF p. 15)
quote: The fourth agency—the Central Intelligence Agency—stated that it did not report contracts due to concerns about the ability of someone to use them to infer agency requirements.
our_interpretation: Contracts of these four agencies are outside our data, so no agency x PSC cells exist for them and government-wide totals understate federal contracting.
test_idea: awarding_agency_name, action_date_fiscal_year: list whether TVA, FDIC, NCUA or any intelligence agency appears as awarding agency in any year FY2008 to FY2025.

claim: CRS says FPDS has no data from judicial branch agencies, the legislative branch, certain DoD components, or some executive agencies such as CIA and NSA.
period_covered: Stated in 2018. Applies to all years.
agencies: Judicial branch, legislative branch, CIA, NSA, certain DoD components
quote: FPDS does not include data from judicial branch agencies, the legislative branch, certain DOD components, or select executive branch agencies—such as the Central Intelligence Agency and National Security Agency.
our_interpretation: Our agency list cannot include these buyers, and DoD totals omit some components with no flag.

claim: GAO found that 49 of 152 agencies in the FY2022 consolidated financial statements did not report to USAspending.gov. Twenty-five of them were executive branch agencies with more than $5 billion in FY2022 net outlays. GAO did not check which of them were required to report.
numbers: 49 of 152 agencies. 25 executive branch. More than $5 billion of $6 trillion in net outlays. Two of the 25 had about $1.2 billion in net outlays and received COVID-19 funds.
agencies: Agencies in the consolidated financial statements
quote: We identified 49 agencies that did not report data to USAspending.gov, 25 of which were from the executive branch and accounted for more than $5 billion in net outlays for fiscal year 2022.
our_interpretation: Net outlays of these agencies are under 0.1% of federal outlays, and GAO does not say whether any of them report contracts to FPDS, so the contract dollars at stake are small but unmeasured.

claim: DoD, HHS and DHS reported $10.9 billion of COVID-19 OTAs in FPDS-NG, but GAO found at least $12.5 billion, a $1.6 billion gap. NIH also obligated about $520 million on COVID-19 OTAs that were not reported in FPDS-NG at all.
numbers: $10.9 billion reported versus at least $12.5 billion actual. $1.6 billion gap. About $520 million NIH OTAs not in FPDS-NG.
quote: In addition to this $1.6 billion, HHS's National Institutes of Health officials told us they obligated about $520 million on COVID-19 OTAs, which were not reported in FPDS-NG.
our_interpretation: Some COVID-19 OTA spending is absent from FPDS altogether, so it cannot appear in our cells under any treatment.

claim: GAO said in 2009 that it could not rely only on FPDS-NG for contracting in Iraq and Afghanistan because not all contract actions were entered. The underlying review was GAO-09-19 from October 2008.
quote: In our October 2008 review of contracting in Iraq and Afghanistan, we could not rely solely on FPDS-NG as a primary source of data because not all contract actions were entered into the system.
our_interpretation: Contingency contracting in FY2008 to FY2010 may be missing from our data, which would understate dollars and vendor counts in DoD, State and USAID cells for the PSCs bought in theater.
test_idea: Track primary_place_of_performance_country_code IRQ and AFG dollars and action counts by awarding agency for FY2008 to FY2012 and look for gaps.

claim: VA OIG warned that VA's File D1 may be incomplete. VA records some contract actions on Form 1358 miscellaneous obligations outside its contract system, and these do not flow to FPDS-NG unless staff import them by hand.
numbers: No dollar figure given. VA quality score 71.50 (Moderate). Only 5 D1 records sampled.
quote: VA must manually import them into FPDS-NG for inclusion in File D1. As a result, there is a greater risk that these transactions may not be accounted for in VA's File D1.
our_interpretation: Some VA purchasing may never reach FPDS, which would shrink VA cell totals and could drop small vendors paid through 1358s.

claim: One OIG recommended its agency limit an accounting system option that skips the automatic creation of an FPDS-NG entry for contract actions.
numbers: One agency (not named in the GAO summary).
quote: one OIG recommended that its agency develop and implement controls to limit the use of an option in its accounting system that bypasses the step to automatically create an FPDS-NG entry when entering contract actions in the accounting system.
our_interpretation: Contract actions can be booked in an agency's accounting system without ever reaching FPDS, which would leave them outside our data.

claim: FAR 4.606(d) says agencies not subject to the FAR may be required by other authority to report to FPDS, and must first get FPDS Program Office approval.
quote: Agencies not subject to the FAR may be required by other authority (e.g., statute, OMB, or internal agency policy) to report certain information to FPDS.
our_interpretation: Coverage of FAR-exempt agencies depends on their own rules, so their presence in our data can start or stop without a FAR change.
test_idea: Columns awarding_agency_code, fiscal_year. List agencies whose row counts start or stop in a given FY.

claim: USAspending lists entities that do not report spending data under the DATA Act. The list includes the legislative branch, the judicial branch (other than the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims), USPS, TVA, the Smithsonian, the Federal Reserve, Amtrak, FHFA and the Intelligence Community Management Account.
numbers: 24 examples listed
agencies: legislative branch, judicial branch, USPS, TVA, Smithsonian and others
pinpoint: About the Data, "Reporting Requirement for Federal Agencies", list "Examples of non-reporting entities include"
quote: Legislative Branch, including Congress, Library of Congress, Architect of the Capitol, the Congressional Budget Office, the Capitol Police, Legislative Commissions and Boards, and the John C. Stennis Center
our_interpretation: The list covers DATA Act account reporting, so it tells us which agencies lack File A to C data, and only some of these bodies also stay out of FPDS.
test_idea: awarding_agency_code, awarding_agency_name. List any rows whose awarding agency is on this non-reporting list (for example Library of Congress, Architect of the Capitol, Smithsonian, USPS, TVA) and sum their dollars by FY.

claim: For Q2 FY2017, GAO found 28 agencies that should have reported DATA Act data but submitted nothing. Seventeen of them showed almost $2 billion in obligations on their SF 133 reports. Thirteen agencies, including DoD and USDA, submitted a File C with no data.
numbers: 28 agencies did not submit. 17 of them held almost $2 billion in obligations. 13 of 78 agencies submitted an empty File C.
quote: Based on the information provided by OMB and the data submitted to Treasury, we identified 28 agencies that should have reported under the DATA Act for the second quarter, fiscal year 2017, but did not submit any data.
our_interpretation: DATA Act file submissions and FPDS reporting are separate channels, so these 28 agencies may still have contract rows in File D1 if they report to FPDS.

claim: One OIG reported that its agency's Q1 FY2019 submission left out almost $10 billion in award-level data for two components. Fourteen of 51 OIGs said their agency's submission was missing data.
numbers: 14 of 51 OIGs reported missing data. One agency missing almost $10 billion for two components.
quote: For example, one OIG reported that its agency’s Q1 FY2019 submission did not include award-level data totaling almost $10 billion for two of the agency’s components.
our_interpretation: GAO does not say whether the missing award data were contracts in FPDS or grants, so the effect on File D1 is unknown.

claim: For the period ending March 31, 2021, 30 agencies submitted a File D1 with no procurement data and 19 of 101 agencies submitted an empty File C. In November 2019 GAO had counted 34 blank File D1 submissions.
numbers: 30 blank File D1. 19 of 101 blank File C. Unreported data about $11.1 billion, 0.22% of obligations.
quote: For the reporting periods ending March 31, 2021, 19 of 101 agencies submitted the file that is to link budget and award information (i.e., File C), and 30 agencies submitted the file that is to contain procurement data (i.e., File D1) with no data in it.
our_interpretation: Blank File D1 submissions come from small agencies with little or no FPDS activity, so few contract dollars are at stake.

claim: Eight agencies in the FY2025 period 12 submission statistics show no publication date, so they filed no DATA Act financial submission for that period. They are VEF, NCD, USICH, FFIEC, the Kennedy Center, ARC, AAHC and OPIC.
numbers: 8 of 111 agencies with recent_publication_date null
pinpoint: results[].recent_publication_date for these 8 agencies (pages 1 and 2). Quote shows the VEF record on page 2
quote: "agency_name":"Vietnam Education Foundation","abbreviation":"VEF","toptier_code":"519","agency_id":1545,"current_total_budget_authority_amount":null,"recent_publication_date":null
our_interpretation: These are small agencies and the gap is in account data, so their FPDS contract rows, if any, are unaffected.

claim: OFPP's FAQ says FPDS has no cut-off date for adding, deleting, changing or fixing an action, and agencies can amend active contracts back to 1980.
numbers: Back to 1980.
quote: Because FPDS is a relational database, there is no cut-off date by which an agency can add, delete, modify, or correct a contract action in FPDS.
our_interpretation: Old fiscal years can change after the fact, so another release of the archive can give different HHI values for the same year.
test_idea: Columns contract_transaction_unique_key, fiscal_year, federal_action_obligation, last_modified_date. Compare totals for one FY across two archive releases.

claim: The acquisition.gov clarification says some simple fixed-price actions can be deobligated after the final invoice without a contract modification. That deobligation shows in File C with no File D1 record.
period_covered: Undated (created 2021-01-04). Applies to DATA Act files from FY2017 on.
quote: Firm fixed price contract actions that meet the simplified acquisition threshold and are not complex can have funds deobligated after the final invoice payment without requiring a contract modification.
our_interpretation: Some unspent money on small fixed-price awards never leaves our D1 totals, which slightly overstates net dollars for small-award vendors.

claim: FPDS warns that it is a real-time database. New actions, modifications and corrections can change data for current and prior fiscal years. DoD data in FPDS is subject to a 90-day delay.
numbers: 90 days
pinpoint: FPDS page "What's New, DoD Data Availability", paragraph 1
quote: Such updates could result in changes to the FPDS-NG data used to compile information reports on actions for current and/or prior fiscal years.
our_interpretation: Our 2026-09-06 snapshot fixes each cell at one point in time, so later corrections to prior years could move vendor shares in a rerun.
test_idea: Compare per-cell net obligations between two archive releases (for example 2026-08 and 2026-09) for FY2008 to FY2024 and list cells whose HHI moves.

claim: GSA's FPDS page says DoD data in FPDS-NG are subject to a 90-day delay and that FPDS updates can change data for current and prior fiscal years.
numbers: 90 days.
period_covered: Undated page, cited by CRS in 2019.
quote: It should also be noted that availability of DoD data entered into FPDS-NG is subject to a 90-day delay.
our_interpretation: Totals for any year can move between releases because FPDS keeps late changes, so our counts are tied to the 2026-09-06 release.

claim: GAO's yearly contracting snapshots use FPDS data pulled six to nine months after the fiscal year ends. The dashboards cite FPDS data as of May 2023 for FY2022, May 2024 for FY2023, June 2025 for FY2024 and April 2026 for FY2025. The FY2018 to FY2020 infographics cite FPDS-NG data for the year with no extraction date.
numbers: FY2022 May 2023. FY2023 May 2024. FY2024 June 2025. FY2025 April 2026. FY2018 to FY2021 no date given.
quote: "sourceDate": "June 2025"
our_interpretation: GAO's totals are early snapshots, so gaps between them and our 2026-09-06 archive for the same year partly reflect late rows and revisions we include.
test_idea: Compare our net federal_action_obligation by FY for FY2018 to FY2025 with GAO's totals ($554.1B, $586.2B, $665.1B, about $637B, $694B, $759B, $755B, $793B) and report the gap by year.

claim: The written authority for DoD's 90-day delay is DFARS PGI 204.604(2). It says DoD contract action reports are not public or open to non-DoD use until 90 days after the Date Signed, to limit risk to military operations.
numbers: 90 days after Date Signed.
period_covered: Current PGI. Present in the PGI revised 2016-09-23.
quote: CARs or their data are not available for public view or for non-DoD use until 90 days after the “Date Signed” data element in order to minimize risk to military operations.
our_interpretation: Our release is dated 2026-09-06, almost a year after FY2025 ended, so the 90-day delay should not cut rows from any year in our window.
test_idea: Columns action_date, last_modified_date, awarding_agency_code. For DoD rows, the gap between action_date and first appearance across releases.

claim: DoD told its Inspector General in 2017 that the 90-day delay had been in place for over 10 years, with OMB and Treasury knowledge, and was documented on the FPDS website.
numbers: Over 10 years as of 2017. Release 91 days after award.
quote: the 90-day delay in releasing FPDS data to the public has been in place for over 10 years, with OMB and Treasury knowledge and is documented on the FPDS website.
our_interpretation: The delay covers our whole window, so DoD rows arrive late in every year from FY2008 on.

claim: GAO reported that FPDS-NG releases DoD procurement data to the public only after a 90-day wait, so DoD contract data reach Beta.USAspending.gov 90 days late. DoD typically accounts for about two-thirds of federal contracting activity. Treasury did not disclose this limitation on the site.
numbers: 90-day delay. DoD about two-thirds of federal contracting activity.
quote: FPDS-NG releases DOD-reported procurement data to the public after a 90-day waiting period, which results in a 90-day delay in reporting these data to Beta.USAspending.gov.
our_interpretation: Our 2026-09-06 release falls well past 90 days after FY2025 ended, so the delay should not truncate FY2025 DoD cells, but any extract taken earlier would undercount DoD.
test_idea: awarding_agency_code, action_date, last_modified_date: compare DoD obligations by action month for July to September 2025 with the same months of FY2024, and the lag from action_date to first appearance.

claim: USAspending says DoD and USACE contract and IDV data are published on a 90-day delay in FPDS itself. The delay carries into USAspending Files C and D1 for these agencies.
numbers: 90 days
pinpoint: About the Data, Sitewide Award Data Disclosures, "Delay in Department of Defense (DOD) Procurement Data", paragraph 1
quote: Procurement data (such as for contracts and indefinite delivery vehicles (IDV)) for the Department of Defense (DOD) and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) are published on a 90-day delay in the
our_interpretation: Release 2026-09-06 is more than 90 days past the end of FY2025, so FY2025 DoD and USACE base rows should be present, but DoD cells in any snapshot taken within 90 days of a period end would be short.
test_idea: awarding_agency_code, action_date, and the monthly delta files (correction_delete_ind). Count DoD FY2025 rows and dollars that first appear in delta files dated after 2025-12-29.

claim: The About page Data Quality section repeats the 90-day DoD and USACE delay and says it also delays File C and subcontract data. It says the disclosure was added because GAO identified the need.
numbers: 90 days
pinpoint: usaspending.gov/about, Data Quality section, first bullet under "The Government Accountability Office (GAO) has identified the need to disclose the following two items"
quote: delaying the availability of procurement, account breakdown by award (File C), and subcontract data on USAspending.gov that pertain to DOD and USACE by 90 days as well.
our_interpretation: This is a publication lag only, so it changes when DoD dollars arrive and leaves the final FY totals unchanged.

claim: GAO again found that the 90-day delay for DoD procurement data was not clearly communicated on USAspending.gov. DoD noted it only in its senior accountable official statement. Its agency profile and transaction queries did not show it.
numbers: 90-day delay.
quote: Specifically, information related to a 90-day delay in data availability for DOD procurement awards is not posted on USAspending.gov.
our_interpretation: The delay changes when DoD rows appear and does not remove them, so a late-2026 release should hold complete FY2025 DoD data.
test_idea: awarding_agency_code, action_date, last_modified_date: share of DoD FY2025 obligations whose last_modified_date is after 2025-12-29.

claim: GAO reported that Treasury, in response to GAO-20-75, added disclosures about the 90-day delay for DoD procurement data on several USAspending.gov pages.
quote: In response to our recommendations, Treasury took steps to improve the disclosure of known data limitations, including providing additional information about the 90-day delay for displaying Department of Defense (DOD) procurement data
our_interpretation: The DoD delay is now a documented feature of the source, so we can cite it as the reason to use a release taken months after fiscal year end.

claim: The FPDS public welcome text says DoD releases contract data only after a 90-day waiting period for security reasons. The same contracts count at once in FPDS aggregate Standard Reports.
numbers: 90 days
pinpoint: FPDS welcome text, section "What's in FPDS-NG?", item "Release of Data"
quote: For security reasons, the Department of Defense (DoD) only releases contract data after a 90-day waiting period.
our_interpretation: FPDS aggregate reports can show DoD totals that the transaction-level feed behind File D1 does not yet hold.

claim: The 90-day sentence is not in PGI 204.604 as revised July 31, 2014. It is in PGI 204.604(2) as revised September 23, 2016. So the PGI text that authorizes the delay dates from 2015 or 2016.
numbers: Absent in the 2014-07-31 revision. Present in the 2016-09-23 revision.
quote: Contract action reports (CARs) must be completed in compliance with the timelines established in FAR 4.604(b)(2) and (3). CARs or their data are not available for public view or for non-DoD use until 90 days after the
our_interpretation: The delay existed in practice long before it was written into the PGI, so the written rule date is no break in our data.

claim: In the PGI revised July 31, 2014, PGI 204.604 is a single unnumbered paragraph on the OSD Procurement Data Improvement Plan. It has no sentence on a 90-day release delay.
period_covered: PGI in force 2014-07-31 until a later revision
quote: PGI 204.604 Responsibilities. The OSD Procurement Data Improvement Plan, posted at
our_interpretation: The written PGI basis for the delay is younger than the delay itself, which DoD dates to about 2007.

claim: CRS says agencies must report award transactions within 30 days, and DoD data may lag longer, generally 90 days.
numbers: 30 days. 90 days for DoD.
quote: There may be a longer lag time with data from the Department of Defense, generally 90 days.
our_interpretation: Our release came 11 months after FY2025 ended, so the 90-day lag should be fully past for all years in our window.

claim: For FY2017 Q2, DoD certified procurement award data for only one day, January 1, 2017. DoD procurement data were not public in FPDS until 91 days after award.
numbers: One day of procurement data certified for the quarter. 91-day delay before public release. 639 procurement award transactions submitted.
quote: the SAO certified procurement award data for only January 1, 2017, which was one day's worth of data, instead of submitting data for the complete quarter.
our_interpretation: The 90-day delay only hides the newest DoD months, and our 2026-09-06 release is more than 90 days past the end of FY2025, so it should not cut FY2025 DoD dollars.
test_idea: Compare DoD FY2025 Q4 dollars in the 2026-09-06 release with an earlier release, if one is kept, to confirm the late quarter is now filled.

claim: DoD OIG found 11,248 untimely data elements in the FY2019 Q1 sample, across 81 of the 385 File D1 transactions. The DoD SAO said DATA Act data come from many systems at different frequencies.
numbers: 11,248 untimely data elements. 81 of 385 D1 transactions and 207 of 351 D2 transactions. D1 timeliness projected error 21.0 percent.
quote: We identified 11,248 instances of untimely data elements across 81 of the 385 File D1 transactions and 207 of the 351 File D2 transactions.
our_interpretation: About one in five sampled DoD contract actions reached FPDS late, which fits our own finding that DoD rows are reported late.
test_idea: Same as the FY2020 Q4 timing test, restricted to FY2019 DoD rows, to check whether the late share fell between FY2019 and FY2020.

claim: DoD entered many contract actions into FPDS-NG later than the FAR deadline of 3 business days after signing. This made 2,083 File D1 data elements untimely.
numbers: 2,238 untimely data elements across 129 of 372 transactions. 2,199 from File D1, of which 2,083 were late FPDS-NG entry. Timeliness projected error 13.6 percent.
quote: 2,083 File D1 data elements were considered untimely because the contract award data in File D1 were not input to FPDS-NG within 3 business days of the award.
our_interpretation: Late entry shifts when a row appears in FPDS but keeps the action date, so it only matters for snapshots taken soon after a fiscal year closes.
test_idea: Compare action_date with initial_report_date (if present in the archive) on DoD rows, and report the share of dollars entered more than 3 business days late by FY.

claim: NASA entered 22 sampled procurement actions into FPDS-NG late. The delayed awards were entered an average of 60 days after the 3-day FAR deadline.
numbers: Timeliness error 8.37 percent on 242 transactions (projected range 1.9 to 7.1 percent as printed). 22 late procurement transactions. 11 File C records not linked to File D1. Average delay 60 days past the deadline.
quote: FPDS-NG awards for these delayed transactions were entered an average of 60 days after the FAR required deadline of 3 days.
our_interpretation: A 60-day lag can push late-September actions out of a snapshot taken right after year end, but our release is a year past FY2025 close.
test_idea: On NASA rows, measure the gap between action_date and initial_report_date (if present) and the share of dollars more than 60 days late by FY.

claim: GSA OIG found 7 sampled File C records that were missing from File D1. Four were late FPDS-NG entries and three had a mistyped award ID.
numbers: 7 records, about 3 percent of the sample of 235. Projected error rates: completeness 3.59, accuracy 4.76, timeliness 2.90 percent. Quality 94.18 points (higher).
quote: The variances were caused by either untimely reporting to FPDS-NG (for four of the records) or incorrect data entry of the Award IDs (for three of the records).
our_interpretation: Wrong award IDs in FPDS would split one contract into two awards but would not change the vendor or the dollars in our cells.

claim: Contract data usually reach USAspending within five days. Contracting officers have three business days to report to FPDS. Two exceptions are the DoD and USACE 90-day delay and a 30-day window for unusual and compelling urgency awards and for actions under FAR subpart 18.2.
numbers: 5 days, 3 business days, 90 days, 30 days
pinpoint: About the Data, "Frequency of Updates to Prime Award Data for Contracts (Procurement)", exceptions list
quote: Publication of Department of Defense (DOD) and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) data in FPDS is delayed 90 days.
our_interpretation: Emergency and urgency contracts can land up to 30 days late, which matters only for snapshots taken near a fiscal year end.

claim: FAR 4.604(b) sets the deadline for a complete contract action report at three business days after award, or 30 days for urgency awards and emergency acquisitions. Reports in draft or error status are not complete.
numbers: 3 business days. 30 days.
period_covered: Current FAR. Same deadlines in the 2012 rule.
quote: CARs in a draft or error status in FPDS are not considered complete.
our_interpretation: Draft or error records are not public, so any action left in draft is missing from our data.

claim: The same clarification says urgent and emergency awards can reach the financial system before FPDS, and emergency flexibilities can delay or waive reporting requirements.
numbers: 3 to 30 days reporting windows.
quote: When such flexibilities are authorized, numerous FAR requirements can be delayed and/or waived to include dollar thresholds, documentation, and reporting requirements, vendor registration requirements, etc.
our_interpretation: Emergency buying (for example COVID-19 in FY2020) can enter FPDS late or with gaps, which affects the cells where it is concentrated.

claim: Treasury officials told GAO that data published in FPDS take 2 days to appear on USAspending.gov.
numbers: 1 day for agency-certified and FABS data. 2 days for FPDS and other external systems.
quote: it takes 1 day for agency-certified data and data published in the Financial Assistance Broker Submission to be incorporated into USAspending.gov, and 2 days for USAspending.gov to reflect data published in other external government-wide reporting systems.
our_interpretation: The USAspending lag after FPDS is negligible next to the DoD 90-day hold and late agency entry.

claim: File D1 data come to USAspending two days after an action is submitted to FPDS.
numbers: 2 days
pinpoint: About the Data, "File D1 (Award and Awardee Attributes (Procurement))", paragraph 2
quote: New data come to USAspending.gov two days after submission to FPDS.
our_interpretation: The pipeline lag from FPDS to USAspending is too short to affect annual cells.

claim: GSA reported in its FY2022 and FY2023 data quality reports that FPDS limitations caused inaccurate values in two key fields, NAICS and Product or Service Code. FPDS does not let agencies change these fields to reflect the most current updates, and OMB had not responded as of December 2024.
numbers: Two fields, NAICS and PSC.
period_covered: FY2022 to FY2023 (reported), unresolved as of December 2024
agencies: GSA (system issue affects all FPDS users)
quote: GSA noted in its fiscal years 2022 and 2023 procurement data quality reports that limitations in FPDS were causing inaccurate information for two FPDS data elements.
our_interpretation: PSC is one of our cell dimensions, so a PSC value frozen at an outdated code can place dollars in the wrong cell or split one market across old and new codes.
test_idea: contract_award_unique_key, modification_number, product_or_service_code, action_date_fiscal_year: share of modification rows whose PSC differs from the base award, and share of rows using PSC codes retired before the action year.

claim: DoD's PSC rule is one code for the predominant amount of supplies or services on the award. CRS warns that a single PSC per contract hides other products or services on it.
quote: Because FPDS contracts are associated with only a single product or service code—even when the contract involves substantial deliveries of other products or services—the analysis in this report should be used only to identify broad overall trends.
our_interpretation: Dollars for mixed contracts sit in one PSC cell, so some cells hold spending for other markets.

claim: The FY2019 summary sampled about 20 FPDS elements against contract files. Product/Service Code matched 98.5% to 99.4% of the time, DUNS 98.6% to 99.8%, Action Obligation 97.5% to 99.7% and Description of Requirement 94.7% to 96.3%. Manual entry was the most common cause of errors.
numbers: PSC 98.5% to 99.4%. DUNS 98.6% to 99.8%. Action Obligation 97.5% to 99.7%. Funding Agency ID 98.0% to 98.7%. Completion date 89.4% to 97.7%
pinpoint: p. 1 (PDF p. 1), section E. Table values from Exhibit 1, p. 2 (PDF p. 2)
quote: Manually entering data was identified as the most frequent challenge to procurement data quality.
our_interpretation: A PSC error rate near 1% means a small share of dollars sits in the wrong PSC cell, which can matter for thin cells.

claim: The acquisition.gov clarification says agencies are not responsible for ultimate parent fields. Parent data come from SAM and Dun and Bradstreet, and errors in them are not the responsibility of procurement officials.
quote: Agencies are not responsible for ultimate parent information since this information is the responsibility of the recipient and is provided automatically to USASpending.
our_interpretation: Our vendor is the parent UEI, a field no agency checks, so parent errors pass straight into vendor shares.
test_idea: Columns recipient_uei, recipient_parent_uei, recipient_parent_name, fiscal_year. Count recipient UEIs mapped to more than one parent UEI within a FY.

claim: M-18-16 says the quality of SAM and subaward data is the legal duty of the award recipient, and agencies do not certify data reported by awardees.
quote: Agencies are not responsible for certifying the quality of data reported by awardees to GSA and made available on USASpending.gov.
our_interpretation: Parent links that come from SAM sit outside agency assurance, which leaves our vendor grouping with no government check.

claim: DoD OIG found the Ultimate Parent Unique Identifier inaccurate or unsupported in all 57 sampled procurement transactions for FY2017 Q2. The report notes this is an FPDS-generated element.
numbers: Ultimate Parent Unique Identifier: 57 of 57 procurement transactions inaccurate or unsupported. Sample of 57 of 639 procurement award transactions.
quote: Ultimate Parent Unique Identifier1 57 N/A
our_interpretation: Our vendor key relies on the parent ID, so a parent field that failed on every sampled DoD record in FY2017 is a direct risk to vendor grouping in the earlier years.
test_idea: On DoD rows by FY, compute the share of dollars with a blank ultimate_parent_uei (or parent DUNS before FY2022) and the share where the parent ID equals the recipient ID.

claim: Inspectors general reviewing Q1 FY2019 data reported Ultimate Parent UEI and parent name errors. One OIG traced them to awardees not keeping their SAM data current. Five OIGs reported completeness error rates above 20% for Ultimate Parent Unique Identifier.
numbers: Ultimate Parent Unique Identifier: 5 OIGs with completeness error over 20%, 13 OIGs with 0%. Ultimate Parent Legal Entity Name: 10 or more OIGs with accuracy error over 20%.
quote: One OIG, for example, reported that errors in Legal Entity Address, Ultimate Parent Legal Entity Name, Ultimate Parent Unique Identifier, and other elements occurred because awardees of the agency’s procurements and grants were not keeping their demographic data current within SAM.
our_interpretation: Our vendor key uses the parent UEI first, so stale or missing parent links can split one firm into several vendors or merge firms, which moves HHI and CR4.
test_idea: recipient_uei, recipient_parent_uei, action_date_fiscal_year: share of obligations with blank parent UEI, and recipients whose parent UEI changes within a year, by agency.

claim: Inspectors general reviewing FY2020 to FY2021 data reported third-party errors in procurement records. Sixteen OIGs reported Ultimate Parent Unique Identifier errors and 22 reported Ultimate Parent Legal Entity Name errors that they attributed to systems such as SAM and FPDS.
numbers: Procurement awards, OIGs reporting third-party errors: Legal Entity Congressional District 24, Ultimate Parent Legal Entity Name 22, Legal Entity Address 18, Awardee Legal Entity Name 17, Ultimate Parent Unique Identifier 16 (Table 4). Third-party sources: SAM 25 OIGs, FPDS 16 (Table 3).
period_covered: One quarter per OIG among FY2020 Q3, FY2020 Q4, FY2021 Q1 and FY2021 Q2
pinpoint: p. 20 (PDF p. 26), Table 4 on p. 21 (PDF p. 27)
quote: Another OIG reported that some inaccuracies related to Ultimate Parent Legal Entity Name and Ultimate Parent Unique Identifier occurred because the third-party system did not properly populate the agency file submission using the correct external system data field.
our_interpretation: Parent UEI errors on contract rows were common across agencies in FY2020 to FY2021, and parent UEI is the first choice in our vendor key.
test_idea: recipient_uei, recipient_parent_uei, recipient_parent_name: for FY2020 to FY2021, count recipient UEIs mapped to more than one parent UEI and recompute CR4 with recipient UEI only to measure the gap.

claim: In the 2021 cycle, 22 of 57 OIGs reported third-party errors in Ultimate Parent Legal Entity Name on procurement awards, second only to Legal Entity Congressional District. One OIG traced parent field errors to a third-party system that filled the agency file from the wrong field.
numbers: OIGs reporting third-party errors for procurement awards: Legal Entity Congressional District 24, Ultimate Parent Legal Entity Name 22, Legal Entity Address 18, Awardee/Recipient Legal Entity Name 17, Ultimate Parent Unique Identifier 16.
period_covered: Mostly FY2020 Q4 or FY2021 Q1
quote: Procurement awards Legal Entity Congressional District 24 Ultimate Parent Legal Entity Name 22 Legal Entity Address 18 Awardee/Recipient Legal Entity Name 17 Ultimate Parent Unique Identifier 16
our_interpretation: Parent fields failed at many agencies through shared systems, so vendor grouping errors in our data are likely government-wide and not limited to one agency.
test_idea: By awarding agency and FY, compute the dollar share where ultimate_parent_uei is blank or equals recipient_uei, and compare the parent-based HHI with a recipient-based HHI.

claim: NASA OIG found 62 sampled transactions with wrong Ultimate Parent Legal Entity Name or Ultimate Parent Unique Identifier. Officials said parent changes made in SAM are not carried into FPDS-NG automatically.
numbers: 62 of 242 tested transactions. NASA accuracy error rate 7.76 percent overall. Quality 95.5 points (Excellent).
quote: Procurement officials explained the errors can occur when an entity updates its registration in SAM, including its address or parent information, but the update is not automatically made in FPDS-NG.
our_interpretation: Parent IDs on FPDS rows can be stale after a merger, so two firms with a new common parent may still count as separate vendors in our HHI and CR4.
test_idea: For each recipient_uei, list distinct ultimate_parent_uei values by FY and action_date, and flag recipients whose parent changes within an award (same PIID).

claim: The DoD sample showed an 11.0 percent accuracy error rate for Ultimate Parent Legal Entity Name and a 1.3 percent rate for Ultimate Parent Unique Identifier. The parent name error rate rose from 0.5 percent in FY2019 Q1.
numbers: Ultimate Parent Legal Entity Name: accuracy 11.0, completeness 0.3, timeliness 15.3 percent (sample rates). Ultimate Parent Unique Identifier: 1.3, 0.0, 15.1 percent. Projected D1 parent name accuracy error 11.1 percent in FY2020 Q4 versus 0.5 percent in FY2019 Q1.
quote: Ultimate Parent Legal Entity Name 11.0 0.3 15.3
our_interpretation: Our vendor key is the parent UEI. The IG found the parent ID field far more accurate than the parent name field, which supports keying on the ID and not on the name.
test_idea: Using ultimate_parent_uei and ultimate_parent_legal_entity_name on DoD rows, count parent UEIs with more than one name per FY and the dollar share they hold.

claim: One OIG found its agency had no clear procedure for recording FPDS-NG transactions after a vendor changed its business identification number. Another OIG traced parent and address errors to awardees not updating SAM.
numbers: One agency each (not named in the GAO summary).
pinpoint: p. 21 (PDF p. 27). Second sentence p. 17 (PDF p. 23)
quote: one OIG reported that the agency lacked clear procedures on the process to record transactions in FPDS-NG when a vendor has changed its business identification number.
our_interpretation: A vendor ID change mid-contract can split one firm into two IDs in our data and lower measured concentration.
test_idea: Count PIIDs whose recipient_uei (or DUNS before FY2022) changes across modifications, and the dollars on those awards by FY.

claim: Vendor name and address in FPDS are fixed at the base award. Task and delivery orders carry the vendor data of the base IDV, and a SAM name change need not trigger a modification.
quote: The task/delivery order contractor information will be aligned to the information on the base (referenced indefinite delivery vehicle) award, not the vendor’s current registration in SAM.
our_interpretation: Mergers and spin-offs can leave orders under the old vendor, which splits or misplaces shares after corporate changes.

claim: The FAC 2005-62 preamble says a generic DUNS such as Miscellaneous Foreign Vendor masks the contractor's identity beyond the local contracting office. The rule set limits on generic identifiers from 2012-12-20.
numbers: Generic use limited to actions at or below $25,000 in 2012 (now $40,000 in FAR 4.605(c)(2)(i)).
agencies: Government-wide, mainly DoD and State overseas
pinpoint: FAC 2005-62, Item I, preamble section I
quote: When a generic DUNS number is used, the identity of the contractor is masked beyond the local contracting office.
our_interpretation: Many foreign vendors pooled under one placeholder act as one large vendor, which inflates HHI and CR4 in overseas cells.
test_idea: Columns recipient_uei, recipient_name, recipient_parent_uei, fiscal_year. Share of dollars per cell on generic UEIs such as LN9PU5M2YZN5.

claim: DoD lists the generic UEIs it allows, including Miscellaneous Foreign Awardees, used for vendors outside the United States with no UEI.
numbers: UEI LN9PU5M2YZN5, CAGE 35KC0.
quote: UEI LN9PU5M2YZN5 – Miscellaneous Foreign Awardees. Used to report actions awarded to vendors located outside the United States providing goods/services when a specific UEI is not available.
our_interpretation: This is the placeholder in our integrity findings, and it is allowed by rule, so it recurs every year.
test_idea: Columns recipient_uei, awarding_agency_code, product_or_service_code, fiscal_year. Drop or split generic UEIs and recompute HHI to measure the change.

claim: DoD purchase card orders under contracts may be filed as consolidated express reports under the generic UEI for GPC Consolidated Reporting, and such reports must use Other than Small Business.
numbers: Generic UEIs R5NWZ87HPLX4 and U9X7H1UVY6U5. Individual reports above $25,000.
period_covered: Current PGI. Same rule with DUNS 136721250 since 2011-09-20.
quote: Note that when a generic UEI is used to report these actions, only “Other than Small Business” is allowed as the “Contracting Officer’s Determination of Business Size” selection.
our_interpretation: Many card vendors can sit under one generic UEI, which creates a false large vendor in DoD supply cells.
test_idea: Columns recipient_uei (R5NWZ87HPLX4, U9X7H1UVY6U5), number_of_actions, product_or_service_code, fiscal_year. Dollars and rows per FY on these UEIs.

claim: An express report sums many actions into one record. The Number of Actions field holds the count, and the obligation fields hold the summed dollars.
period_covered: Current PGI. Same rule since at least the 2011-09-20 revision.
quote: When express reports are used, sum all of the actions and enter in the “Number of Actions” data field.
our_interpretation: Row counts understate true actions wherever express reports are used, so action counts should use number_of_actions.
test_idea: Columns number_of_actions, fiscal_year, awarding_agency_code. Compare row counts with the sum of number_of_actions by FY.

claim: HHS ASPR reported its COVID-19 OTAs in the FPDS-NG procurement contract module instead of the OTA module. GAO said this overstated ASPR's COVID-19 procurement contracts by $1.55 billion as of March 14, 2021.
numbers: $1.55 billion in ASPR OTA obligations recorded as procurement contracts
quote: FPDS-NG reflects overreporting of ASPR's COVID-19 procurement contracts by $1.55 billion and no dollars obligated on ASPR's COVID-19 OTAs in the OTA module.
our_interpretation: These OTA dollars likely sit in our File D1 rows as HHS contracts in FY2020 and FY2021, which would add a few large vaccine or medical awards to HHS cells and could raise HHI and CR4 there.
test_idea: Filter awarding_sub_agency for ASPR in FY2020 to FY2021 and search transaction_description for OTA or other transaction, then sum dollars and recompute HHI for the affected PSC cells with and without them.

claim: FPDS-NG showed one consortium management firm receiving $7.2 billion in COVID-19 OTAs. GAO found the firm passed nearly all of it to five pharmaceutical companies, each receiving $450 million to $2 billion.
numbers: $7.2 billion through one firm. Five companies at $450 million to $2 billion each. About 58 percent of the $12.5 billion went through consortia.
quote: In actuality, the management firm distributed nearly all of the awarded dollars to five pharmaceutical companies, with each receiving $450 million to $2 billion.
our_interpretation: Recipient fields can name an intermediary instead of the performing firms, which would overstate one vendor's share and inflate HHI in any cell where such awards appear.
test_idea: List the top recipient names by PSC cell for DoD and HHS in FY2020 to FY2021 and check whether consortium managers such as Advanced Technology International appear among contract rows.

claim: Three of the top five prototype OT recipients in FPDS-NG were consortium management firms. FPDS-NG did not show which consortium members carried out the projects.
numbers: Total $7,225.9 million prototype OT obligations FY2016 to FY2018
quote: Three of the top five recipients were consortium management firms
our_interpretation: The recipient on consortium awards is a pass-through manager, so a vendor-share measure over such awards would show false concentration.
test_idea: Check whether recipient names Advanced Technology International, Consortium Management Group or National Center for Manufacturing Sciences appear in our contract rows and with what dollars by FY and PSC.

claim: In the FPDS OTA recipient field, DoD staff typically enter the consortium management organization. FPDS had no field naming the consortium, and before June 2022 no field for the consortium members doing the work.
numbers: $24.3 billion on consortia-based OTAs went to 12 CMOs representing 28 consortia, FY2019 to FY2021
period_covered: FY2019 to FY2021, with an FPDS change in June 2022
quote: For example, while FPDS includes a data field for tracking OTA recipients, DOD personnel typically enter in the names of the CMOs. FPDS does not include a separate data field for systematically tracking the consortium.
our_interpretation: Any OTA dollars in our data would credit a handful of management organizations instead of the firms doing the work, which would inflate HHI and CR4 in the DoD research and prototype PSC cells.
test_idea: Look for OTA rows. For any found, list top recipient names and parent UEIs by FY and check whether a few management organizations dominate.

claim: FPDS added consortium fields in 2022. GAO then checked FY2023 and FY2024 OTA records tied to known consortium managers. DoD filled them correctly for 2,036 of 2,431 records (84 percent). The other 395 records still named the consortium manager as the vendor performing the work.
numbers: 2,036 of 2,431 correct (84 percent). 395 wrong, about $911 million or 6 percent of DoD consortia-based OTA obligations.
quote: The remaining 395 records inaccurately list the consortium management organization as the vendor performing work.
our_interpretation: Vendor identity on consortium awards is still wrong for about 6 percent of dollars even after the June 2022 fix, which matters only if OTA rows enter our cells.

claim: GAO said in 2009 that interagency contracts could not always be identified in FPDS-NG because of how they were coded. It also found the major program field at DHS was typically blank and some contracts were wrongly coded as time-and-materials or as commercial services.
quote: we found that it was not always possible to identify interagency contracts in FPDS-NG because of how these contracts are coded.
our_interpretation: Interagency buying that cannot be flagged reliably means we cannot cleanly separate assisted acquisitions from an agency's own buying in a cell.

claim: GAO said in 2003 that many FPDS errors come from data entry mistakes by agency contracting staff. It also found FPDS coded 1,034 contracts worth $325 million as HUBZone awards to firms SBA had not certified, and missed 1,712 HUBZone contracts worth $589 million.
numbers: 1,034 contracts ($325 million) miscoded as HUBZone. 1,712 contracts ($589 million) not coded as HUBZone.
quote: Our work and that of agency inspectors general indicates that many of the errors in FPDS are due to data entry mistakes by agency contracting personnel.
our_interpretation: Our measure keys on vendor and dollars, so the socioeconomic flag errors matter little. The named cause, manual entry by contracting staff, is a standing risk for any field we use across FY2008 to FY2025.

claim: GAO traced a random sample of 385 FY2012 awards on USASpending.gov back to agency records. Only 2% to 7% of awards matched agency records on all 21 data elements GAO tested.
numbers: 2% to 7% fully consistent (95% confidence). 4% of the 385 sampled awards. Sample held 153 contracts and 232 assistance awards (Table 8, p. 38). Award amount 88% to 94% consistent, 3% to 7% inconsistent. NAICS (contracts only) 72% to 85% consistent, 10% to 22% inconsistent (Table 9, p. 39).
quote: GAO estimates with 95 percent confidence that between 2 percent and 7 percent of the awards contained information that was fully consistent with agencies’ records for all 21 data elements examined.
our_interpretation: The record-level failure rate mostly reflects address, title and place-of-performance fields, and GAO did not test PSC, so the effect on PSC-based cells in FY2012 is not measured.

claim: For Q2 FY2017, GAO estimated that only 0% to 1% of award records were fully consistent with agency sources, down from 2% to 7% in its 2014 review. Budgetary records did much better at 56% to 75%.
numbers: Award records fully consistent: 0% to 1%. Budgetary records: 56% to 75%. Sample of 402 records from 24 CFO Act agencies, 106 of them procurement (Table 3). Excludes Primary Place of Performance address lines, which would have made the award figure zero (footnote 37).
agencies: 24 CFO Act agencies (procurement and assistance combined)
quote: In contrast, we estimate that only between 0 and 1 percent of the award records were fully consistent with agency sources.
our_interpretation: The fully consistent measure fails on any one of 26 fields, most of which our measure does not use, so it overstates the error risk for obligation, agency and vendor fields.

claim: For Q4 FY2018, GAO estimated that 24% to 34% of award transactions were fully consistent with agency sources, up from 0% to 1% in Q2 FY2017. GAO saw the gain despite a stricter definition and more fields tested.
numbers: Award transactions fully consistent 24% to 34%. Significantly consistent 62% to 72%. Budgetary 84% to 96%. Sample of 405 records, 158 of them procurement. All data 99% to 100% complete and 90% to 93% accurate.
agencies: All agencies that submitted by February 11, 2019 (procurement and assistance combined)
quote: we estimate with 95 percent confidence that between 84 and 96 percent of the budgetary transactions and between 24 and 34 percent of the award transactions in the USAspending.gov database were fully consistent with agency sources.
our_interpretation: Record-level quality improved sharply between FY2017 and FY2018, which is a reason to check whether any HHI or CR4 shift around FY2017 to FY2018 is a data artifact.

claim: At the element level for Q4 FY2018, Federal Action Obligation was 91% to 97% consistent and Awarding Agency Name 98% to 100%. NAICS got worse than in Q2 FY2017, with 23% to 38% of procurement records inconsistent. PSC and parent UEI were not tested.
numbers: Federal Action Obligation 91% to 97% consistent, 1% to 6% inconsistent. Awarding Agency Name 98% to 100%. Awardee Legal Entity Name 96% to 99%. NAICS 62% to 76% consistent, 23% to 38% inconsistent (was 68% to 85% and 7% to 20%). 18 of 35 award elements significantly consistent, 5 of 35 significantly inconsistent (Table 4, p. 52 to 53).
pinpoint: p. 17 (PDF p. 23), Table 4 on p. 52 (PDF p. 58)
quote: Eighteen of the 35 award data elements and subelements in our sample were significantly consistent in Q4 FY2018, compared to only one of 26 data elements and subelements we tested in our 2017 review.
our_interpretation: Obligation amounts and awarding agency, which set our weights and agency dimension, were highly consistent, while industry codes like NAICS stayed weak, which hints that PSC may also carry coding error.

claim: At the data element level in Q2 FY2017, only Awarding Agency Name was significantly consistent among 26 award elements. Federal Action Obligation was 84% to 92% consistent. NAICS was 68% to 85% consistent and Current Total Value of Award only 33% to 52% for procurement awards. PSC was not tested.
numbers: Awarding Agency Name 92% to 97% consistent. Federal Action Obligation 84% to 92% consistent, 1% to 6% inconsistent. NAICS (procurement only) 68% to 85% consistent, 7% to 20% inconsistent. Current Total Value of Award (procurement only) 33% to 52% consistent, 41% to 61% inconsistent. Funding Agency Code 55% to 66% consistent. 11 of 26 elements significantly inconsistent (Table 4, p. 61).
pinpoint: p. 21 (PDF p. 26), Table 4 on p. 61 (PDF p. 66)
quote: In contrast, just 1 of the 26 data elements and subelements relating to awards—Awarding Agency Name—met this criterion.
our_interpretation: The two fields that define our dollar weights and our agency dimension tested well, while PSC, the other cell dimension, was never tested by GAO.

claim: OMB said the 24 CFO Act agencies self-certified FPDS data as 97.68% accurate and 99.14% complete and timely on average for FY2017 to FY2022. GAO separately found DOE's sampling not statistically valid and GSA's sampling procedures not documented in enough detail.
numbers: 97.68% accurate, 99.14% complete and timely, 25 key data elements, FY2017 to FY2022 average.
period_covered: FY2017 to FY2022 (self-certified), FY2023 (GAO review of procedures)
pinpoint: p. 2 (PDF p. 7), p. 18 to 19 (PDF p. 23 to 24)
quote: agencies self-certified that the procurement data submitted to FPDS were, on average, 97.68 percent accurate and 99.14 percent complete and timely for 25 key data elements.
our_interpretation: The high self-certified rates rest on agency samples that GAO found flawed at some agencies, so we should treat them as an upper bound.

claim: HHS and VA reported FPDS accuracy below their own 95% target for several key fields in FY2021 to FY2023 and documented no corrective action plans. HHS dollar value fields were near 80% accurate.
numbers: HHS Date Signed 77.9%, 75.9%, 88.4%. HHS Base and All Options Value 81.8%, 79.2%, 81.0%. HHS Base and Exercised Options Value 82.1%, 80.1%, 78.5%. VA Date Signed 97.5%, 87.9%, 89.1%. VA Estimated Ultimate Completion Date 98.3%, 83.4%, 83.6% (FY2021, FY2022, FY2023, Table 1).
quote: neither agency documented corrective action plans for FPDS data elements that scored below this threshold for consecutive years (see table 1).
our_interpretation: The weak fields are dates and contract ceiling values, while Action Obligation and PSC do not appear in the low-accuracy table, so our measure is less exposed.

claim: OFPP in 2009 found the FY2008 sampling guidance too weak to measure the accuracy of specific data elements by agency, and agencies sampled in inconsistent ways.
quote: the FY 2008 guidance was not sufficient for determining the accuracy of specific data elements by agency with the statistical precision required by our guidance.
our_interpretation: The FY2008 accuracy statements are weaker than later years, which is one more reason to treat FY2008 cells with care.

claim: OFPP's required accuracy test is agency-wide. The sample must give 95% confidence with no more than 5 points of error for the whole agency, with element rates for fields such as Action Obligation, Funding Agency ID, PSC and DUNS.
numbers: 95% confidence, plus or minus 5 percentage points.
period_covered: FY2009 data on (2009 memo), repeated in 2011.
quote: The sample design and sample size must be sufficient to produce statistically valid conclusions for the overall department or agency at the 95% confidence level, with a margin of error of no more than ±5 percentage points.
our_interpretation: Agency-wide accuracy says little about any single agency by PSC cell, so certified accuracy does not cover our unit of analysis.

claim: GAO reported that its 2010 review found every one of 100 sampled awards on USASpending.gov had at least one data error, and grants from programs at nine agencies were missing for FY2008.
numbers: 100 of 100 sampled awards had at least one error. Programs at nine agencies missing for FY2008.
quote: Also, from a sample of 100 awards on USASpending.gov, each award had at least one data error and the website did not include information on grants from programs at nine agencies for fiscal year 2008.
our_interpretation: The first year of our panel had no clean award records in GAO's small sample, which supports treating FY2008 cells with extra caution.
