claim: GAO found the parent DUNS number inconsistent with agency records for 26% to 35% of FY2012 awards. GAO said nearly all of these cases were assistance awards, because the field was not displayed for assistance awards.
numbers: Parent DUNS inconsistent for 26% to 35% of awards. Nearly all were assistance awards.
quote: The Parent DUNS number, used to uniquely identify parent entities (if applicable) doing business with the government, contained inconsistent information for 26 percent through 35 percent of awards.
our_interpretation: Our vendor key is the parent identifier on contract rows, and GAO tied this error to assistance awards, so the FY2012 contract parent field looks less affected than the headline rate suggests.
test_idea: recipient_parent_uei or parent DUNS, recipient_uei, action_date_fiscal_year: share of FY2008 to FY2012 obligations with a blank parent ID, and count of distinct parent IDs per recipient ID per year.

claim: GAO summarized 53 inspector general reports on Q2 FY2017 data. Only 15 OIGs found their agency data generally complete, timely, accurate, or of quality. GAO said the OIG error rates are not comparable and no government-wide rate can be projected.
numbers: 15 of 53 OIGs found data generally complete, timely, accurate, or of quality (6 of 24 CFO Act, 9 of 29 non-CFO Act). 38 of 53 did not. 21 OIGs reported error rates over 50% for 25 data elements.
quote: Based on the OIG reports, we found that 15 of the 53 OIGs determined that their agencies’ data were generally complete, timely, accurate, or of quality, comprising 6 CFO Act agency OIGs and 9 non-CFO Act agency OIGs (see fig. 3).
our_interpretation: The OIG results describe whole submissions and mix contracts with grants, so they do not give a usable error rate for contract obligations.

claim: For FY2017 Q2, 15 of 53 OIGs found their agency's data generally complete, timely, accurate or of quality. The other 38 did not.
numbers: 15 of 53 (6 of 24 CFO Act and 9 of 29 non-CFO Act, from Figure 3). 38 of 53 not. Over half of 40 sampling OIGs projected accuracy errors of 25 percent or more, 8 above 75 percent.
quote: 15 of the 53 OIGs determined that their agencies' data were generally complete, timely, accurate, or of quality
our_interpretation: First-cycle error rates were high but pool many files and fields, and GAO says they cannot be combined into one rate.

claim: GAO said the FY2017 Q2 OIG error rates are not comparable across agencies and cannot be projected to a government-wide rate.
numbers: 40 OIGs sampled, 9 tested all transactions, 4 did no testing.
quote: the overall error rates are not comparable and a government-wide error rate cannot be projected.
our_interpretation: IG error rates should not be averaged or compared across agencies in our write-up.

claim: For FY2019 Q1, 37 of 51 OIGs reported higher quality data under a 20 percent error benchmark, and 11 reported moderate or lower quality. Fourteen OIGs said some components' or systems' data were missing.
numbers: 37 of 51 higher quality. 11 moderate or lower. 47 on time. 14 with missing component or system data.
quote: 37 of 51 OIGs reported that their agencies' data were of higher quality, and 11 OIGs reported data quality that was of moderate or lower quality
our_interpretation: These counts describe whole submissions and do not isolate File D1, so they give no contract-specific rate.

claim: In the 2021 cycle, 45 of 57 OIGs rated their agency's DATA Act data excellent or higher. Eight rated it moderate and four rated it lower.
numbers: 27 excellent, 18 higher, 8 moderate, 4 lower, of 57 OIG reports.
period_covered: Mostly FY2020 Q4 or FY2021 Q1 (agency choice)
quote: Most (45 of 57) OIGs reported that the overall quality levels of data agencies submitted were “excellent” or “higher”
our_interpretation: The ratings cover whole submissions, so they show broad improvement but give no field-level number for our use.

claim: DoD OIG projected error rates of 6.5 percent for accuracy, 0.7 percent for completeness and 13.6 percent for timeliness for DoD's FY2020 Q4 award data. These rates pool File C (financial) with Files D1 and D2 (award) data elements.
numbers: accuracy 6.5 percent, completeness 0.7 percent, timeliness 13.6 percent. Sample of 372 transactions from 438,603 File C transactions. 304 of the 372 came from the Defense Logistics Agency stratum (358,731 transactions).
quote: Files C, D1, and D2 projected error rates were 6.5 percent for accuracy, 0.7 percent for completeness and 13.6 percent for timeliness.
our_interpretation: These are pooled rates over many descriptive and dollar fields, so they say little about the obligation, agency and vendor fields that drive our HHI and CR4.

claim: Most DoD errors sat in File D1 and came from how data was entered into FPDS-NG. Of 3,429 errors found in Files C, D1 and D2, 3,179 were in File D1.
numbers: 3,179 of 3,429 errors (92.7 percent) in File D1. File C 192 errors. File D2 58 errors.
quote: Of the 3,429 errors we identified in Files C, D1, and D2, 3,179 (92.7 percent) were attributable to File D1 and primarily occurred because data was inaccurately or untimely entered into FPDS-NG.
our_interpretation: The error source is FPDS data entry, which is the same source as our archive, so any field error found here is also in our rows.

claim: DoD OIG rated the DoD FY2020 Q4 DATA Act submission as moderate quality. It scored 80 of 100 points on the CIGIE scorecard.
numbers: 80.0 of 100 points. Data element accuracy 28.0 of 30, completeness 14.9 of 15, timeliness 13.0 of 15.
quote: the DoD submission scored 80 out of the 100 maximum points possible.
our_interpretation: The rating is a whole-submission score and cannot be mapped to any one field we use.

claim: For DoD's FY2019 Q1 submission, File D1 had projected error rates of 0.5 percent for completeness, 13.4 percent for accuracy and 21.0 percent for timeliness. DoD OIG rated DoD procurement data as moderate quality.
numbers: File D1: completeness 0.5, accuracy 13.4, timeliness 21.0 percent. File D2: 17.9, 33.9, 59.0 percent. Sample of 385 D1 transactions from 953,806. Quality moderate for procurement, low for grants.
quote: File D1 (procurement) data elements projected error rates for completeness, accuracy, and timeliness were 0.5 percent, 13.4 percent, and 21.0 percent, respectively.
our_interpretation: This is the only DoD cycle with D1-only projected rates, and the near-zero completeness rate means sampled D1 rows rarely had blank required fields.

claim: DoD reported Federal Action Obligation correctly on most sampled contract transactions. The sample error rate was 3.0 percent (11 of 369), with an absolute error of $27.5 million in the sample.
numbers: PIID Federal Action Obligation: 358 accurate, 11 not accurate, 369 tested, 3.0% error, $27,512,818.32 absolute value of errors. Potential Total Value of Award: 11.0% error, $806,547,899,855.29 absolute value of errors.
quote: PIID DE 13 Federal Action Obligation 358 11 0 369 3.0% $27,512,818.32
our_interpretation: The dollar field we sum had a low sample error rate, while the cumulative value fields we do not use carried the very large dollar errors.

claim: DoD OIG found NAICS Code wrong in 138 sampled transactions. In 112 of them the contract documents did not show a code at all.
numbers: NAICS Code accuracy error 37.4 percent (sample). 112 of 138 because the award documents had no code. 26 because File D1 did not match the documents.
quote: Of the 138 inaccurate North American Industrial Classification System (NAICS) Codes, 112 were considered inaccurate because the contract award documentation did not include a code
our_interpretation: Product or Service Code does not appear among the data elements DoD OIG tested in Table 5, so this IG work gives no accuracy figure for the PSC field that defines our cells.

claim: DoD management objected that the FY2019 Q1 statistical sample was mostly Defense Logistics Agency procurement data and did not reflect all of DoD.
numbers: No figure in the quoted passage. The FY2020 Q4 audit later drew 304 of 372 sampled transactions from the Defense Logistics Agency stratum.
quote: stating that it resulted in the review of mostly Defense Logistics Agency procurement data, which does not reflect all of the DoD.
our_interpretation: The DoD error rates mostly describe high-volume Defense Logistics Agency orders, which may not carry over to the large-dollar service and weapons contracts that dominate many DoD cells.

claim: DHS OIG found DHS procurement data elements of high quality for FY2020 Q4. Procurement correctness rates were 99.4 percent for completeness, 89.3 percent for accuracy and 99.4 percent for timeliness.
numbers: Procurement (45 records): completeness 99.4%, accuracy 89.3%, timeliness 99.4%, quality 94.4% (High). Whole submission 84.7 of 100 (moderate).
quote: Accuracy 89.3% 83.3% 85.9% High
our_interpretation: DHS contract data scored better than the DHS submission overall, which was pulled down by FEMA grant data.

claim: DHS OIG found 14 procurement data elements with inaccurate data at least 10 percent of the time because of weak DHS controls.
numbers: 14 procurement and 15 financial assistance elements at or above 10 percent. 19 of 51 elements (37 percent) on the combined sample. 12 of 51 (24 percent) at 20 percent or more.
quote: we found that 14 procurement and 15 financial assistance data elements had inaccurate data at least 10 percent of the time attributed to a lack of DHS controls.
our_interpretation: The report does not say which of the 14 procurement elements are dollar or vendor fields, so the effect on our measure cannot be sized from this passage.

claim: DOE OIG rated DOE's FY2021 Q1 data excellent at 98.9 points. The sample error rates were 1.53 percent for completeness, 2.70 percent for accuracy and 0.01 percent for timeliness.
numbers: 98.9 points. Completeness 1.53%, accuracy 2.70%, timeliness 0.01% (sample). 447 procurement and 17 financial assistance records. Only 253 of 905 errors (28 percent) attributable to DOE.
quote: the Department earned an “excellent” quality score of 98.9 points
our_interpretation: DOE contract rows look reliable for the fields that matter to us in this quarter.

claim: HHS OIG rated HHS's FY2021 Q1 data excellent at 99 points. The projected accuracy error rate was 1.45 percent, and 36 period of performance dates in Files D1 and D2 did not match the documents.
numbers: 99 points. Accuracy 1.45% (1.22% to 1.68%). Completeness 0.55%. Timeliness 0.55%. 269 samples. Period of performance exceptions: 21 start date, 10 end date, 5 potential end date.
quote: The projected error rate for the accuracy of the data elements is 1.45%.
our_interpretation: HHS rates pool contracts and grants, and the dates found wrong are not used in our measure.

claim: GSA OIG projected a 4.76 percent accuracy error rate for GSA's FY2021 Q1 data elements. The most common error, Legal Entity Congressional District, came from a flaw in how File D is derived from FPDS-NG.
numbers: Accuracy 4.76 percent (95 percent interval 1.82 to 7.70). Completeness 3.59 (1.00 to 6.18). Timeliness 2.90 (0.54 to 5.26).
quote: The projected error rate for the accuracy of the data elements is 4.76 percent.
our_interpretation: GSA, which runs FPDS, had low error rates on its own contract data in this quarter.

claim: VA OIG rated VA's FY2020 Q4 submission moderate at 71.50 points. Only 5 of the 45 sampled records came from File D1, and one had a wrong Ultimate Parent Legal Entity Name caused by an entity other than VA.
numbers: 71.50 points. Sample 45 records: 5 from D1, 40 from D2. D1 exceptions: 1 Ultimate Parent Legal Entity Name, 1 Period of Performance Start Date.
quote: VA scored 71.50 points, which is a quality rating of Moderate.
our_interpretation: Five D1 records are too few to say anything about VA contract data quality for our measure.

claim: DOE's Current Total Value and Potential Total Value of Award fields in FPDS did not match agency records on 114 and 136 records. DOE linked this to FPDS errors made before the DATA Act and carried forward on management and operating contracts.
numbers: 114 Current Total Value errors and 136 Potential Total Value errors. Spending data may be misstated by at least $34 billion across 15 procurement awards.
quote: accuracy issues related to the Current Total Value of Award and Potential Total Value of Award data elements were likely a result of FPDS-NG recording errors made prior to the enactment of DATA Act reporting requirements.
our_interpretation: We should keep using transaction obligations and never the cumulative value fields, which carry old errors on DOE's large management and operating contracts.
test_idea: For DOE awards, compare the sum of federal_action_obligation per PIID with the latest base_and_exercised_options_value and flag awards where they differ by more than $1 billion.

claim: NASA contracting officers followed the FPDS-NG definition of Current Total Value of Award, which differs from the DATA Act definition. Errors hit 85 sampled File D1 transactions worth $4 billion.
numbers: 85 File D1 transactions, $4 billion. Potential Total Value errors totaled $847 million.
quote: For the dollar value-related data element Current Total Value of Award, we found errors in 85 tested File D1 transactions totaling $4 billion.
our_interpretation: This confirms that the cumulative value fields follow FPDS rules and should not stand in for obligations in our measure.

claim: OIGs reported Current Total Value and Potential Total Value errors caused by known calculation issues within FPDS.
numbers: Potential Total Value and Current Total Value had the highest absolute dollar errors of all monetary elements (37 of 57 OIGs reported monetary element errors).
period_covered: Mostly FY2020 Q4 or FY2021 Q1
quote: some OIGs reported errors in the monetary data elements Current Total Value of Award and Potential Total Value of Award because of known calculation issues within FPDS.
our_interpretation: These are cumulative fields that we do not sum.

claim: For Q1 FY2019, 27 OIGs reported errors in Federal Action Obligation on procurement awards, totaling about $84 million in absolute value. The largest dollar errors were in Potential Total Value of Award, about $384 billion.
numbers: Procurement: Potential Total Value of Award 29 OIGs, $383,602,276,812. Current Total Value of Award 28 OIGs, $9,329,393,508. Federal Action Obligation 27 OIGs, $84,017,274 (Table 1). Not projectable.
pinpoint: p. 17 (PDF p. 23), Table 1 on p. 18 (PDF p. 24)
quote: OIGs reported Potential Total Value of Award and Current Value of Award as the monetary data elements with the highest absolute dollar values of errors for Q1 FY 2019.
our_interpretation: Our measure sums Federal Action Obligation, and the errors found there were small in dollars compared with the ceiling-value fields we do not use.

claim: One OIG found its agency misused the Transaction Obligated Amount standard to report deobligations. Fifteen OIGs reported procurement Federal Action Obligation errors totaling about $64 million in absolute value.
numbers: Procurement: Potential Total Value of Award 26 OIGs, $828,464,250,023. Current Total Value of Award 25 OIGs, $7,008,967,549. Federal Action Obligation 15 OIGs, $64,469,238 (Table 2).
quote: an agency improperly used the data standard for the Transaction Obligated Amount to report deobligations
our_interpretation: Errors in the obligation field we sum were small in dollars, and the deobligation misuse concerns File C, while our data come from File D1.

claim: The FPDS Action Obligation element records the net amount obligated or de-obligated by each transaction. De-obligations carry a minus sign.
numbers: none
pinpoint: Element 3C Action Obligation, Instruction, p. 39 (PDF p. 41)
quote: Enter the net amount of funds (in dollars and cents) obligated or de-obligated by this transaction. If the net amount is zero, enter zero. If the net amount is a de-obligation, enter a minus sign in addition to the net amount.
our_interpretation: Negative vendor totals in a cell are a documented feature of net obligation data, which our findings already flag.

claim: GAO compared FPDS-NG competition coding with contract files for 107 contracts and orders and found 19 coded incorrectly, about 18 percent. Nine coded as not competed had been competed, and 10 coded as competed with one offer were either not competed or had more than one offer.
numbers: 19 of 107 miscoded (about 18 percent). 9 of 79 coded noncompetitive were competed. 10 of 28 coded competed with one offer were wrong. One Army contract coded one offer had three offers and another had four.
period_covered: Contracts at locations chosen on FY2008 obligations. Trend data FY2005 to FY2009.
agencies: Army, Navy, Air Force, DHS (Secret Service, ICE), Interior
quote: Specifically, 19 of the 107 contracts and orders we reviewed, or about 18 percent, were coded incorrectly.
our_interpretation: Our HHI and CR4 use only vendor and dollars, so competition coding errors do not change them, but any check that pairs concentration with extent competed or number of offers inherits an error rate near 18 percent in this nonrandom sample.
test_idea: Cross-tab extent_competed against number_of_offers_received and flag rows coded competed with offers missing or zero, or not competed with offers above 1, by FY.

claim: Five of the nine contracts wrongly coded as not competed were orders under single-award IDIQ contracts that had been competed. The orders were coded as not competed.
numbers: 5 of 9
quote: Another 5 of the 9 miscoded noncompeted contracts were actually orders under single-award IDIQ contracts that were competed, but the orders were coded as not competed.
our_interpretation: Order-level competition codes may not match the parent award, so any competition variable we attach to a cell should come from the parent IDV where possible.
test_idea: For orders under single-award IDVs, compare the order extent_competed with the parent IDV extent_competed (via parent_award_id_piid) and count mismatches by FY.

claim: GAO checked 35 high-dollar DoD awards coded in FPDS-NG as competed with one offer and found 10 coded wrongly, worth $271.8 million. Six were noncompetitive awards and four had received multiple offers. GAO judged DoD's one-offer data not sufficiently reliable.
numbers: 10 of 35 miscoded ($271.8 million). 6 actually noncompetitive. 4 had multiple offers. DoD IG separately found 27 percent of 107 FY2011 one-offer awards miscoded.
period_covered: Awards issued April 1, 2011, to March 31, 2012 (FY2011 Q3 to FY2012 Q2). DoD IG sample FY2011.
quote: Based on our analysis of 35 one-offer awards, 10 awards totaling $271.8 million were incorrectly coded in FPDS-NG.
our_interpretation: Number of offers is unreliable at DoD around FY2011 to FY2012, so it should not be used to validate or explain DoD cell concentration in those years.
test_idea: For DoD rows FY2011 to FY2012, count rows with number_of_offers_received equal to 1 and extent_competed in the not competed codes, and report that share by FY.

claim: GAO said its sample covered large-dollar awards that get more review, so errors may be more common among other awards. GAO still found DoD competition data reliable enough for overall trend analysis.
quote: However, as described in this report and later in this appendix, we found the data on one-offer awards not sufficiently reliable.
our_interpretation: Field-level error found in large awards likely understates error in the many small rows that dominate our action counts.

claim: GAO found 28 of 62 sampled contracts coded in FPDS-NG as noncompetitive under the urgency exception when they were not. Twenty of the 28 had used simplified acquisition procedures instead.
numbers: 28 of 62 miscoded. 20 of the 28 used simplified procedures. 3 Air Force contracts used other exceptions.
period_covered: FY2011 to FY2012 sample. FY2010 to FY2012 trends.
quote: Nearly half—28 of the 62 contracts in GAO's sample—were incorrectly coded as having used the urgency exception when they did not.
our_interpretation: The reason not competed field is unreliable at these agencies in FY2011 to FY2012, so it should not be used to split cells into urgent and routine buying.
test_idea: Count rows whose other_than_full_and_open_competition code is the urgency exception and whose award value is under the simplified acquisition threshold, by agency and FY.

claim: GAO found DoD, DHS and HHS misreported competition data in FPDS-NG for 22 of 41 IT orders it reviewed. Most were competed orders coded with an exception to fair opportunity, which put competition data on about $3 billion a year of IT orders in doubt.
numbers: 22 of 41 orders miscoded (DoD 11, HHS 6, DHS 4 of the 21 citing follow-on or other statutory authority). About $3 billion a year affected. 29 of 171 sampled noncompetitive actions were actually competed.
period_covered: FY2016 sample. FY2013 to FY2017 trends.
quote: misreported competition data in the Federal Procurement Data System-Next Generation (FPDS-NG) for 22 of the 41 orders GAO reviewed. GAO's findings call into question competition data associated with nearly $3 billion in annual obligations for IT-related orders.
our_interpretation: Competition fields on orders are least reliable exactly where our cells hold many IDV orders, so a competition covariate in IT PSC cells would overstate noncompetitive buying.
test_idea: For orders under multiple-award IDVs in IT PSCs (D and 70 codes), tabulate fair_opportunity_limited_sources values such as follow-on action and other statutory authority by agency and FY.

claim: Between $10 million and $148 million a year of IT obligations in FPDS-NG carried no competition code at all.
numbers: $10 million to $148 million a year
quote: Between $10 million and $148 million annually did not include a code for competition.
our_interpretation: Blank competition codes are a small share of dollars and do not affect vendor shares.
test_idea: Sum dollars with extent_competed blank by FY and PSC group.

claim: FPDS-NG records only whether the base OT awarded to a consortium was competed. Modifications that fund consortium projects keep the base award's competition code, even when the projects were competed among members.
numbers: FPDS-NG showed 48 percent of prototype OT obligations competitively awarded, FY2016 to FY2018. DoD officials said this understates competition.
quote: DOD senior contracting officials stated that FPDS-NG tracks only whether the base transaction was competitively awarded and that modifications made to transactions awarded to consortiums automatically retain the same competitive or non-competitive designation as the base contract.
our_interpretation: Competition codes on modifications can reflect the base award only, so any competition variable built from modification rows may misstate how a cell's dollars were competed.
test_idea: For contract rows, compare extent_competed on modifications (modification_number not 0) with the base action of the same award and report the share that always match by FY.

claim: GAO found 8 of 244 other transactions wrongly coded as prototype OTs in FPDS-NG. Until June 2019 FPDS-NG could not tell prototype from production OTs, so DoD reported both as prototype.
numbers: 8 of 244 miscoded (4 production, 4 experimental). $7.2 billion on prototype OTs FY2016 to FY2018.
quote: According to Defense Pricing and Contracting officials, until June 2019, DOD did not have the ability to differentiate between prototype and production other transactions in FPDS-NG; therefore, both prototype and production other transactions were reported as prototype other transactions.
our_interpretation: OT type labels before June 2019 cannot be trusted, which matters only if we try to bring OTA spending into our cells.

claim: Comparing FPDS with DoD and consortium manager data, GAO found OTA obligations both underreported and overreported in FPDS. Some consortia-based OTAs were not in FPDS at all.
period_covered: Prototype OTAs FY2019 to FY2021. Production OTAs June 29, 2019, to September 30, 2021.
quote: we identified a number of data inaccuracies in FPDS, including underreporting and overreporting of obligations.
our_interpretation: OTA totals in FPDS are not a reliable count of OTA spending, so any OTA adjustment to our measure would carry unknown error.

claim: The FPDS-NG OTA module had no National Interest Action field, so agencies had no systematic way to flag an OTA as COVID-19 related. The procurement module does have that field. DoD did not flag $52.5 million on the Pfizer OTA and DHS did not flag $25.5 million on two OTAs as COVID-19 related.
numbers: $52.5 million (DoD Pfizer OTA, November 2020). $25.5 million (DHS CWMD, February to September 2020).
quote: the module does not have a systematic way for agencies to identify an OTA as COVID-19-related. The procurement contract module of FPDS-NG, in contrast, includes a National Interest Action data field that allows tracking of COVID-19 contracts.
our_interpretation: COVID-19 flags exist only for procurement module rows, so any COVID-19 sensitivity check on our FY2020 to FY2022 cells must use the NIA code and cannot cover OTAs.

claim: GAO used the National Interest Action code to find COVID-19 contract actions but said some coded actions held obligations not specific to the pandemic. It removed such obligations for actions over $1 million. GAO also noted prior inconsistencies in how these codes were opened and closed after earlier disasters.
numbers: COVID-19 NIA code established March 13, 2020, then set to expire September 30, 2020. Cleanup applied to actions over $1 million.
period_covered: FY2020 (data as of June 11, 2020). Prior disaster review April 2019 (2017 hurricanes).
pinpoint: p. 11 (PDF p. 15) and pp. 2 to 3 (PDF pp. 6 to 7)
quote: In April 2019, we identified inconsistencies in establishing and closing these codes following previous disasters or emergencies, which could have implications for the use of the National Interest Action code for tracking contract actions and associated obligations in response to COVID-19
our_interpretation: The NIA code both over-captures and under-captures COVID-19 dollars, so a COVID-19 exclusion test on FY2020 to FY2022 cells using it is only approximate.
test_idea: Recompute FY2020 and FY2021 HHI and CR4 with and without rows whose national_interest_action_code is the COVID-19 code and also with disaster_emergency_fund_codes for COVID-19, and compare the two exclusions.

claim: GAO found in February 2021 that over $1.2 billion in USDA Farmers to Families Food Box obligations were not reported with the COVID-19 National Interest Action code. USDA later went back and coded the earlier actions.
numbers: Over $1.2 billion
quote: For example, in February 2021, we found that over $1.2 billion in obligations for the program were not reported with the COVID-19 National Interest Action (NIA) code.
our_interpretation: USDA food cells in FY2020 to FY2021 may carry COVID-19 dollars without the NIA flag in older extracts, though our 2026 archive should reflect the retroactive fix.
test_idea: For USDA AMS rows in FY2020 to FY2021 with food PSCs, compare dollars carrying the COVID-19 NIA code with total dollars and check whether the food box awards carry the code.

claim: OMB required a Disaster Emergency Fund Code in financial files for contracts funded by COVID-19 supplemental money and a separate NIA code in FPDS-NG for all COVID-19 procurement actions. GAO said the two are not tied, so an award can carry one without the other, and USAspending's DEFC-based COVID-19 totals do not capture all COVID-19 procurement.
quote: However, use of the NIA code is not necessarily tied to COVID-19 supplemental appropriations. As a result, awards with the COVID-19 NIA value may not have a COVID-19 DEFC value, and vice versa.
our_interpretation: Any COVID-19 sensitivity test on our cells gives different answers depending on whether it uses the NIA code or the DEFC, so we should run both and report the range.
test_idea: Cross-tab rows by COVID-19 NIA code and COVID-19 DEFC values for FY2020 to FY2022 and report dollars in each of the four combinations.

claim: GAO found the FPDS-NG base and all options value reported far below the true contract value in several cases, and five contracts since October 28, 2009, listed with a value of zero. One Army contract worth about $84 million was reported at $24 million, and two related Army contracts listed at zero were worth $350 million.
numbers: $84 million reported as $24 million. Two contracts at zero actually $350 million. Five zero-value awards since October 28, 2009.
agencies: Army and other agencies awarding 8(a) sole-source contracts
quote: For instance, the Army had awarded a contract worth about $84 million according to contract documents, but its reported value in FPDS-NG was only $24 million.
our_interpretation: Our shares use obligated dollars, so errors in the base and all options value do not move HHI or CR4, but any filter or weight built on contract ceiling value would inherit these errors.
test_idea: Count base award rows (modification_number 0) with base_and_all_options_value equal to 0 while federal_action_obligation is positive, by agency and FY.

claim: GAO estimated that NNSA and six of its M&O contractors wrongly reported $1.1 billion of $16.8 billion in small business awards in FY2018 to FY2022 as going to small businesses. For another $1.9 billion GAO could not tell whether the business was small.
numbers: $1.1 billion of $16.8 billion misreported (conservative estimate). $1.9 billion undeterminable. Average M&O subcontract about $32,000. Average NNSA prime contract to small business about $2.3 million.
quote: GAO estimates that the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) and six of its management and operating (M&O) contractors incorrectly reported $1.1 billion of their $16.8 billion in small business contracts awarded in fiscal years 2018–2022.
our_interpretation: Most of these dollars are M&O subcontracts that never enter FPDS, so the misreporting mainly affects DOE's small business goaling figures and not our vendor shares.

claim: In FY2015 the IDV type was missing for $0.06 billion of defense obligations and $0.3 billion of civilian obligations in FPDS-NG.
numbers: $0.06 billion defense. $0.3 billion civilian.
quote: Note: The type of IDV was missing for a small number of contract obligations—$0.06 billion for defense agencies and $0.3 billion for civilian agencies.
our_interpretation: Missing IDV type is a tiny share of dollars and does not affect vendor shares.

claim: Minority-owned flags in FPDS-NG come from business owners' self-identification in CCR, which GAO could not independently verify. In FY2011 data, firms tagged with a specific minority group but not flagged as minority-owned made up less than 3 percent of cases.
numbers: Less than 3 percent internally inconsistent
quote: we analyzed the FPDS-NG data to determine cases in which contracting firms were identified as belonging to a particular minority group, such as Subcontinent Asian, but did not designate the firm as being minority-owned. This occurred in less than 3 percent of the cases.
our_interpretation: Socioeconomic flags are self-reported and lightly checked, so they should only be used as rough descriptors of vendors in a cell.
test_idea: Count rows where a specific minority-group flag is true but the minority-owned business flag is false, by FY.

claim: FPDS has no field showing whether an approved nonmanufacturer rule waiver was used on a contract. GAO said this leaves no way to tell whether waivers helped agencies meet small business goals.
quote: However, as there is no data field in FPDS to indicate whether an approved NMR waiver was used for a contract, there is no mechanism to indicate whether NMR waivers were used in helping agencies to achieve those goals.
our_interpretation: Small business set-aside rows for manufactured goods may hide large manufacturers behind small resellers, so vendor identity in those product cells reflects the reseller.

claim: GAO found DoD's FY2023 report to Congress on FAR production contracts that followed prototype OTAs was unreliable. Only 7 of 48 contracts DoD listed were actual follow-on production contracts.
numbers: 7 of 48 (15 percent)
quote: We found that DOD's reporting of FAR production contracts in its annual report to Congress for fiscal year 2023 was unreliable and inaccurate.
our_interpretation: There is no reliable flag for FAR contracts that follow an OTA prototype, so we cannot trace prototype winners into our production cells.

claim: Procurement committee officials told GAO that some agencies purposely changed dates in FPDS so that expired contracts would not appear active in service contract inventory reports. GAO said this leads to inaccurate FPDS data.
period_covered: Reported during the March 2024 to September 2025 audit
quote: As a result, to avoid having expired contracts appear in service contract inventory reports, PCE officials stated that some agencies have purposely changed dates in FPDS, leading to inaccurate FPDS data.
our_interpretation: The altered fields appear to be contract end dates, and our fiscal year comes from the action date, so the measure is probably not affected.

claim: GAO reported that some indefinite delivery contracts carried the wrong award type because the FPDS-NG data dictionary did not match the data feed the broker used. Treasury said it was building a workaround and could not change FPDS-NG itself.
quote: For example, the incorrect award type was reported for some indefinite delivery contracts.
our_interpretation: Award type is not part of our cell key or vendor key, so this matters only for any split of results by award type.
test_idea: award_type, idv_type, parent_award_id_piid: count rows with a parent IDV but an award type that is not an order, by fiscal year.

claim: DoD reported the vendor's own address as the primary place of performance on 232 of 385 sampled contract actions. DoD followed a DFARS PGI instruction that differs from the OMB and Treasury definition.
numbers: 256 D1 transactions with Primary Place of Performance Address errors. 232 used the Legal Entity Address. Projected accuracy error 66.5 percent for this element in FY2019 Q1 and 6.8 percent in FY2020 Q4 (DODIG-2022-027 Table 7).
quote: listed the Legal Entity Address instead of the Primary Place of Performance Address for 232 transactions
our_interpretation: Place of performance is not part of our measure, so this only matters for any later geographic split of DoD cells.

claim: DoD put Federal Action Obligation amounts into the Current Total Value and Potential Total Value fields in FPDS for FY2017 Q2.
numbers: No count given in the quoted passage.
quote: the DoD reported Federal action obligation amounts for procurement award data in the Current Total Value and the Potential Total Value elements in FPDS.
our_interpretation: We sum federal_action_obligation and do not use the total value fields, so this misuse does not touch our dollars.

claim: DHS described the reason for a modification, such as deobligating funds, in the award description instead of the goods or services bought.
numbers: No count in the quoted passage.
quote: for award modifications, officials described the reason for the modification (e.g., deobligate funds) instead of describing the goods or services being procured.
our_interpretation: We classify by PSC and not by description text, so this matters only for any text-based check of PSC codes.

claim: DOE OIG found 314 procurement records missing Legal Entity Congressional District. The broker did not extract this field from FPDS-NG into File D1 as designed.
numbers: 314 procurement records. Completeness error rate 1.53 percent overall.
quote: we identified 314 procurement award records that were not populated with the Legal Entity Congressional District code.
our_interpretation: This is an extraction gap between FPDS and the broker in a field we do not use.

claim: The USAspending Data Dictionary says the FPDS agencyID inside the contract transaction key is the agency that submitted the record, which often differs from the awarding agency.
numbers: none
quote: agencyID is an FPDS field that captures the Agency or SubTier Agency that submitted the transaction to FPDS (often distinct from the awarding agency).
our_interpretation: Our agency key is the awarding agency code, so the submitting agency does not affect cell assignment.

claim: USAspending says award descriptions have been persistently hard for agencies to keep accurate. Some are too long, too technical, coded, or empty.
numbers: none
pinpoint: About the Data, "Award Description Data Quality", paragraph 2
quote: Maintaining data quality for the award description field has been persistently challenging for federal agencies.
our_interpretation: We do not use descriptions.

claim: The FY2024 and FY2025 dashboards drop missing or other values from their figures. GAO says these values are less than one percent of total obligations.
numbers: Less than 1 percent of obligations
quote: values that represent less than one percent of total obligations.
our_interpretation: Blank or other categorical values are under 1 percent of dollars in GAO's view, which suggests that PSC or agency blanks in our data are a small share of dollars in recent years.
test_idea: Sum dollars with blank product_or_service_code or awarding_agency_code by FY and check that the share is under 1 percent for FY2024 and FY2025.

claim: CRS found two fiscal year fields on DoD prototype OT records that users fill in different ways. One record shows $115 million obligated in FY2020 for an agreement signed in February 2016.
numbers: $115 million. FY2013 to FY2017 records reviewed.
quote: FPDS-NG records an obligation of $115 million in FY2020 for this agreement.
our_interpretation: OT rows can sit in the wrong fiscal year, so cells with OT dollars may shift between years.
test_idea: Columns action_date, action_date_fiscal_year, award_type_code. For OT rows, count cases where the fiscal year does not match the action date.

claim: GSA restructured all R&D PSCs in the October 2020 revision. It end-dated 721 R&D codes on October 29, 2020 and activated 155 new R&D codes on October 30, 2020, aligned to OMB budget functions.
numbers: 721 R&D PSCs end-dated (720 four-character codes plus category rows in the GSA spreadsheet). 155 new R&D PSCs. Old scheme had 7 stage digits (1 to 7). New scheme has 5 (1 to 5). 13 new two-letter areas (AA to AS).
period_covered: Change on October 30, 2020 (FY2021, about one month into the fiscal year)
agencies: Government-wide, R&D buyers (DoD, DOE, NASA, HHS)
pinpoint: Section V.C, Research and Development Code Summary item 3, p. 5 (PDF p. 8)
quote: Seven Hundred twenty-One (721) R&D PSCs are being end-dated on October 29, 2020 by new R&D codes starting with
our_interpretation: R&D cells in FY2021 to FY2025 use broad budget-function codes while FY2008 to FY2020 cells use narrow program codes, so R&D HHI and CR4 are not comparable across the October 2020 break.
test_idea: product_or_service_code starting with A, action_date. Count distinct R&D codes and dollars by FY. Flag FY2021 rows dated October 1 to 29, 2020 that still carry old codes.

claim: The new R&D codes reuse many old code strings with a different meaning. AC11 meant defense aircraft basic research until October 29, 2020 and means all Department of Defense military basic research from October 30, 2020.
numbers: The GSA spreadsheet shows 139 of the 155 new R&D code strings were also used by an ended code. 581 old code strings were retired with no same-string successor. AC15 changed from aircraft operational systems development to DoD R&D facilities and major equipment.
period_covered: FY2008 to FY2020 versus FY2021 to FY2025
pinpoint: Appendix 1, Research and Development Codes END-DATED (October 2020), p. 187 (PDF p. 190)
quote: AC11 (R&D- DEFENSE SYSTEM: AIRCRAFT (BASIC RESEARCH))
our_interpretation: A cell keyed on the string AC11 silently changes from one narrow market to a much wider one in FY2021, so a jump in vendors or dollars there is a coding artifact.
test_idea: product_or_service_code. For the 139 reused strings, compare dollars and vendor counts in FY2020 and FY2022 per agency. Large jumps confirm the meaning change.

claim: The PSC Manual revision effective October 1, 2011 (start of FY2012) renumbered the facility-based service codes. GSA reports 384 ended service codes replaced by 504 new codes, 30 new service codes, 12 service codes ended by merging into existing codes, and 39 product codes ended.
numbers: 384 service codes ended and replaced by 504 new codes. 30 new service codes. 12 service codes ended (combined). 39 product codes ended. The GSA spreadsheet shows 2,445 code rows end on 2011-09-30 and 2,544 start on 2011-10-01. 436 code strings ended with no same-string successor and 535 strings are new.
pinpoint: Section V.A, Summary of Changes to PSC Codes, p. 9 (PDF p. 10)
quote: 384 ended codes were replaced with 504 new codes (captured new and/or expanded numbering scheme for facility codes)
our_interpretation: Cells keyed on a facility-based service code (C1xx, Y1xx, Z1xx, Z2xx and similar) in FY2008 to FY2011 have no one-to-one successor in FY2012 to FY2025, so a PSC-level time series breaks at FY2012.
test_idea: product_or_service_code, action_date_fiscal_year. List codes with obligations only in FY2008 to FY2011 and codes that first appear in FY2012, with dollars per side.

claim: The 2011 revision split the old combined maintenance, repair and alteration codes into two codes. Code Z111 for office buildings became Z1AA (maintenance) and Z2AA (repair or alteration).
numbers: One old code (Z111) maps to two new codes (Z1AA, Z2AA). 73 facility types in 15 categories.
pinpoint: Section V.D, Services Code Summary item 2, p. 11 (PDF p. 12)
quote: Now, this service is split into two codes: Z1AA represents
our_interpretation: A facility maintenance market measured under one code before FY2012 is split across two cells after, so each new cell has fewer vendors and dollars than the old one and HHI can rise by construction.
test_idea: product_or_service_code. Compare FY2011 dollars and vendor counts in Z111 with FY2012 dollars and vendor counts in Z1AA plus Z2AA for each awarding agency.

claim: End-dated PSCs cannot be chosen for new reports in FPDS, but rows already reported keep the old code. Historical rows in our data therefore carry whatever code was valid when they were reported.
pinpoint: Section V.B, General Comments item 6, p. 10 (PDF p. 11)
quote: The ended codes can no longer be selected in FPDS, but the legacy data are retained.
our_interpretation: Old codes stay on FY2008 to FY2011 and FY2012 to FY2020 rows, so any crosswalk has to be applied by us and is not done in the source data.
test_idea: product_or_service_code, action_date. Count rows dated after each code END DATE in the GSA spreadsheet. A nonzero count shows modifications that kept a retired code.

claim: The same October 2020 revision replaced the IT codes with a new schema. GSA end-dated 40 IT service codes and 30 IT product codes and activated 23 IT service codes and 17 IT product codes.
numbers: 40 IT service and 30 IT product codes end-dated. 23 IT service and 17 IT product codes added. GSA spreadsheet shows D301 to D399 and 7010 to 7050 ending and DA01 to DK10 and 7A20 to 7K20 starting on October 30, 2020.
pinpoint: Section V.D, Services Code Summary item 2, p. 5 (PDF p. 8)
quote: Activated 23 new IT service PSCs (codes) and 17 new IT product PSCs (codes). These new IT codes have a new schema.
our_interpretation: IT cells (D3xx and 70xx before, Dxxx letter codes and 7A to 7K after) break at FY2021 and need a many-to-many crosswalk.
test_idea: product_or_service_code starting with D or 70 or 7A to 7K. Dollars by code family by FY for FY2019 to FY2022.

claim: GAO found that Treasury does not tell users that the completeness and comparability of award data vary across years because standards, requirements, validations and reviews changed. Users can pull FY2008 to FY2021 data with no note on how quality differs.
numbers: About 57% of Legal Entity Congressional District values for procurement awards did not follow the current two-digit format.
quote: For example, while a user is able to search for award data from fiscal years 2008 through 2021 for any given agency, there is no information about how the quality of that data may differ because of changes in guidance and requirements over time.
our_interpretation: Our panel spans exactly this period, so trends in HHI and CR4 can partly reflect changes in reporting rules.
test_idea: action_date_fiscal_year with product_or_service_code, recipient_parent_uei, funding_agency_code: per-year share of blank or invalid values, to flag years with format breaks.

claim: USAspending warns that reporting requirements change over time and that more recent fiscal years tend to have higher quality data. OMB guidance issued since 2010 changes the completeness and consistency of specific elements over time.
numbers: none
pinpoint: About the Data, "Changes in Reporting Requirements", paragraph 1
quote: More recent fiscal years tend to have higher quality spending data than older fiscal years.
our_interpretation: Trends in HHI from FY2008 onward may partly reflect better vendor and PSC coding in later years.
test_idea: Null or invalid rates of recipient_uei, recipient_parent_uei and product_or_service_code by FY.

claim: The FPDS dictionary revision of 4/2/2022 removed element 9A Unique Entity ID (DUNS) and made 9M Unique Entity ID the primary entity key. GSA says all its systems stopped using DUNS on April 4, 2022.
numbers: switch date April 4, 2022
quote: Removed data element 9A Unique Entity ID (DUNS). Updated data element 9M Unique Entity ID as the primary entity key.
our_interpretation: Vendor identity before April 2022 rests on UEIs mapped back from DUNS, so any mapping gaps could split or merge vendors across the break.
test_idea: recipient_uei, recipient_parent_uei, action_date. Null rates by month from FY2020 to FY2023, and vendors whose parent UEI changes at the April 2022 break.

claim: GSA says all registered entities had their new UEI from June 2021, and that SAM.gov and other GSA systems would no longer use the DUNS number from April 4, 2022.
numbers: more than 2.5 million UEIs generated
pinpoint: GSA news release of March 16, 2022, paragraph 1
quote: This means SAM.gov and other GSA systems will no longer use the DUNS number for identifying entities.
our_interpretation: Same break as the FPDS dictionary change, seen from the SAM side.

claim: USAspending switched recipient grouping from DUNS to UEI in March 2022. It also fixed a bug that had kept recipients with null DUNS from flowing from the Broker.
numbers: none
pinpoint: Release notes, March 22nd, 2022, API and Technical Notes, "Unique Entity Identifier (UEI) updates"
quote: Updated Recipient Lookup ETL to utilize UEI in place of DUNS for grouping recipients
our_interpretation: Recipient and parent fields in older rows were regrouped after the fact, so parent assignments in FY2008 to FY2021 reflect 2022 logic.
test_idea: recipient_parent_uei vs recipient_uei by FY. Share of rows where parent UEI is blank and recipient UEI is filled, before and after FY2022.

claim: USAspending warned in 2018 and 2019 that a parent recipient can change over time and that a child recipient name could replace the ultimate parent name.
numbers: none
pinpoint: Release notes, October 31, 2018, Website Updates, "Updated the Recipient Profile"
quote: Users can now see connections to more than one Parent recipient when the Parent recipient has changed over time.
our_interpretation: A vendor whose parent changes inside a fiscal year can be split across two parent IDs in one cell, which lowers measured concentration.
test_idea: recipient_uei with more than one recipient_parent_uei inside one FY. Count and dollars.

claim: On October 21, 2019 USAspending stopped grouping USACE Civil Works under DoD. Archive downloads filtered on DoD stopped including USACE.
numbers: none
pinpoint: Release notes, October 21, 2019, Website Updates and Fixes
quote: Downloads in award data archive, custom award download or custom account download where DOD is used as an agency filter will no longer include USACE data.
our_interpretation: USACE Civil Works rows should carry their own awarding agency code across all years in a 2026 file, though a mix of 096 and 097 would split one agency into two cells.
test_idea: awarding_agency_code and awarding_sub_agency_name for USACE rows by FY. Check that USACE Civil Works never appears under 097.

claim: USAID and State told Congress in March 2025 that they would reorganize foreign assistance programming. State officials told GAO that State has no access to information on terminated contracts held in USAID legacy systems.
pinpoint: Footnote 10, p. 4 (PDF p. 8), repeated in Appendix I footnote 3, p. 35 (PDF p. 39)
quote: In March 2025, USAID and State notified Congress of their intent to undertake a reorganization of foreign assistance programming.
our_interpretation: USAID (072) contract dollars may move to State (019) cells late in FY2025 and in later releases, so USAID and State cells are not comparable to earlier years.
test_idea: awarding_agency_code 072 and 019, action_date. Monthly dollars and action counts for FY2024 and FY2025, and any USAID-originated PIIDs reported under State.

claim: Executive Order 13869 moved the primary responsibility for government-wide background investigations from OPM to the Department of Defense. The NBIB transition period ended on or before September 30, 2019.
numbers: Transition period ending on or before September 30, 2019 (so DoD from FY2020).
quote: requires that the primary responsibility for conducting background investigations Government-wide be transferred from the Office of Personnel Management to the Department of Defense.
our_interpretation: Contracts for investigation services could move from OPM cells to DoD cells at FY2020, so OPM market size drops and DoD gains a new market without any change in buying.
test_idea: awarding_agency_code 024 and 097, product_or_service_code for investigative services. Dollars and vendor lists by FY for FY2017 to FY2022.

claim: GAO said in 2005 that no system tracked total spending through other agencies' contract vehicles and services. GSA said FPDS-NG was not meant to collect data on financial transactions between agencies.
quote: However, total spending using other agencies' contracting vehicles and services is unknown because there is currently no system that tracks and reports this information.
our_interpretation: Our cells use the awarding agency, so dollars bought for one agency through another agency's vehicle land in the awarding agency's cell, which can merge different buyers' markets into one cell.
test_idea: Compare awarding_agency_code with funding_agency_code per cell and report the share of dollars where they differ, by FY.

claim: GAO found that Treasury does not validate award fields it imports from external systems such as FPDS and did not disclose this. GAO found procurement records whose start date fell after the end date and almost 8,000 procurement records with meaningless award descriptions.
numbers: Almost 8,000 procurement records with nondescriptive award descriptions since 2017. Thousands of procurement records over the 250-character FPDS limit after June 28, 2019.

our_interpretation: Treasury passes FPDS values through unchecked, so the quality of PSC, vendor and obligation fields in our data rests only on FPDS rules and agency review.

our_interpretation: Treasury does not validate FPDS rows, so field errors in vendor or PSC codes pass straight into our cells.

our_interpretation: File D1 values reach our data as FPDS recorded them, so any FPDS entry error passes straight into our cells.

claim: GSA paused IAE modernization in September 2023 for lack of resources. In FY2023, IAE operating cost was about $168 million against agency contributions of about $68 million, a gap of nearly $100 million. FPDS is one of three legacy systems with no modernization plan.

quote: In fiscal year 2023, for example, the operating cost for the IAE was approximately $168 million and agencies’ total contribution was approximately $68 million, leading to a gap of nearly $100 million.
our_interpretation: FPDS fixes that agencies request, such as the PSC and NAICS limitation, have little chance of being made while the system is frozen.

claim: None of the 24 CFO Act agencies' FY2023 procurement data quality reports met all relevant OMB requirements. Nineteen of 24 missed the deadline, three by more than 180 days. OMB tracks reports only for CFO Act agencies and has no monitoring procedures.
numbers: 0 of 24 met all requirements. 19 of 24 late. 3 more than 30 days late, 3 more than 180 days late. Deadline is 120 days after fiscal year end.
quote: In addition, 19 of the 24 CFO Act agencies did not meet the deadline for submitting the report. For example, three agencies submitted their reports more than 30 days late, and another three agencies submitted their reports more than 180 days late.
our_interpretation: The annual accuracy certifications that back FPDS data are weakly enforced, so self-reported accuracy cannot stand in for an outside error rate.

claim: Of 70 agencies that reported FY2023 data to FPDS, only 36 (51%) confirmed completing the annual procurement data quality report. Of the other 34, 23 said they did not complete one and 11 did not respond. The 34 held almost $2 billion, about 0.26% of FY2023 contract obligations.
numbers: 36 of 70 (51%) confirmed. 23 did not complete, 11 did not respond. 34 agencies held almost $2 billion, about 0.26% of $759.2 billion. 30 of the 34 were executive branch. The 36 include all 24 CFO Act agencies.

our_interpretation: Agencies without a quality check hold a tiny share of dollars, but their cells may be less reliable and could be flagged.
test_idea: awarding_agency_code, federal_action_obligation, action_date_fiscal_year: list FY2023 awarding agencies outside the 24 CFO Act agencies and their share of dollars.
