claim: For Q4 FY2018, DoD's File C included data from only 6 of its 18 accounting systems, about $2.2 billion of the $117 billion in its Files D1 and D2.
numbers: 6 of 18 accounting systems. File C about $2.2 billion, just under 2% of $117 billion in D1 and D2.
quote: According to DOD officials, its File C submission for Q4 FY2018 included data from six of its 18 accounting systems.
our_interpretation: File C only links contract rows to budget accounts, and our measure uses File D1 obligations, so missing File C does not drop DoD contract rows.

claim: GAO said in 2005 that GSA had not told users how accurate and complete agency data in FPDS-NG were. In 2009 GAO said this information was still not readily available on the FPDS-NG website.
quote: Information on the accuracy and completeness of FPDS-NG data is not readily available through the FPDS-NG website.
our_interpretation: Users of FY2008 era data had no published accuracy figure from GSA, so we cannot attach an official error rate to early years of our window.

claim: OMB in 2004 said GAO had found FPDS data not timely or accurate, and asked agencies to connect contract writing systems to FPDS-NG by the end of FY2005.
numbers: Deadline end of FY2005.
quote: the data that departments and agencies submit to the Federal Procurement Data System (FPDS) are not sufficiently timely or accurate.
our_interpretation: Agencies still moving to automated reporting in the mid-2000s can explain uneven coverage in FY2008.

claim: OFPP in 2007 required statistically valid, independent verification of FPDS data and said the government had struggled to get contract data right for decades.
numbers: Annual statement due 2007-12-15.
quote: The government has struggled with getting contract data right for decades.
our_interpretation: Formal data checks only start with FY2007 data, so FY2008 is among the first checked years.

claim: OFPP required data quality plans for FY2008 FPDS data and a certification by January 5, 2009 that FY2008 data were in FPDS.
numbers: Plans due 2008-07-15. Certification due 2009-01-05.
quote: By January 5, 2009, agencies shall certify that their agency's FY 2008 procurement data is in FPDS and that their data quality plans have been completed.
our_interpretation: A push to load all FY2008 actions into FPDS by early 2009 may have added late rows to FY2008.

claim: DoD components send their annual certification and data validation results for the prior fiscal year to DPC by December 15. DPC sends one consolidated DoD certification to OMB by January 5.
numbers: December 15. January 5.
quote: By December 15th of each year, the chief acquisition officer of each DoD component required to report its contract actions shall submit to the Principal Director, Defense Pricing, Contracting, and Acquisition Policy, its annual certification and data validation results for the preceding fiscal year
our_interpretation: The certifications exist for each year but are not public in the sources we opened, so we cannot use them to grade cells.

claim: OFPP's 2011 guidance kept annual certification each January of the prior fiscal year's FPDS records to OFPP and GSA.
quote: agency Chief Acquisition Officers must certify annually each January to the Office of Federal Procurement Policy (OFPP) and the General Services Administration (GSA) that their previous fiscal year's FPDS records are complete and accurate.
our_interpretation: The process covers completeness at agency level only.

claim: M-15-12 says procurement data sent to USAspending from FPDS follow existing FAR reporting and annual verification rules, and any change to FPDS reporting goes through rulemaking.
quote: Procurement data, as provided to USAspending.gov from the Federal Procurement Data System (FPDS-NG or Integrated Award Environment successor), shall follow existing regulatory requirements for reporting and annual verification and validation.
our_interpretation: The DATA Act did not change what contracts are reported, so the FAR scope rules above hold across our window.

claim: The acquisition.gov clarification says express reporting gives one FPDS record but many financial obligations, and that financial adjustments such as discounts, penalties and interest are not reported in FPDS.
quote: Such reporting will result in one contract action record in FPDS but multiple financial obligations in the financial system (for example, purchase of prosthetics).
our_interpretation: File D1 rows and dollars will not match agency financial records, and our dollars follow FPDS only.

claim: CRS warns that FPDS data may be unreliable and that a query can return different results depending on parameters and timing. CRS uses FPDS only for broad trends and rough estimates.
quote: In some instances, a query for particular data may return differing results, depending on the parameters and timing.
our_interpretation: Our results are best framed as trends with known gaps.

claim: CRS says USAspending results may be incomplete or contain inaccuracies and points to GAO findings through September 2025.
quote: these results may also be incomplete or contain inaccuracies.
our_interpretation: Congress's own research arm treats the data we use as imperfect, which supports listing these caveats with our results.

claim: In 2005 GAO found that DoD had delayed connecting its contract writing systems to FPDS-NG at least twice. DoD then held about 60 percent of FPDS-NG contract actions and expected full connection only in FY2006.
numbers: DoD about 60 percent of contract actions. Full connection expected sometime in FY2006.
quote: Given that DOD data represent about 60 percent of the contracting actions that will be captured within FPDS-NG, this delay significantly affects the ability of FPDS-NG to reflect timely and accurate procurement data.
our_interpretation: This is background for FY2008 only. DoD feeder systems were still new to FPDS-NG shortly before our window opens, which may help explain DoD reporting quirks we found in FY2008.

claim: In June 2022 the agencies updated FPDS to record whether an OTA is consortium-based and which members perform the work. GAO notes that FPDS updates are resource constrained and need a majority vote of 24 agencies to be funded.
numbers: Change date June 2022. 24 voting agencies.
quote: In June 2022, the agencies updated FPDS to track which consortium members are performing the work and whether OTAs are consortium-based or not.
our_interpretation: A member-level vendor exists only for OTA actions after June 2022, so any OTA vendor fix we attempt cannot cover FY2019 to FY2022.

claim: GAO recommended that GSA add FPDS-NG controls so contract values are recorded accurately. GSA officials said no contract award should ever have a value of zero.
quote: GSA officials who are responsible for managing the FPDS-NG data system told us that there should not be any instances in which a contract award would have a value of zero.
our_interpretation: FPDS-NG allowed implausible values to pass its edit checks in FY2008 to FY2012, so validation rules alone do not guarantee clean dollar fields in our early years.

claim: FPDS-NG let contracting officers enter a competition code on single-award orders that differed from the parent contract. DHS said GSA expected to prefill these codes in FY2019 Q1, which would not fix multiple-award order errors.
numbers: GSA fix expected first quarter of FY2019
period_covered: FY2016 sample, system change expected FY2019 Q1
quote: However, as FPDS-NG currently operates, contracting officers have the ability to input a different competition code for these orders.
our_interpretation: Order competition codes may change behavior around FY2019 because of a system prefill, which could create a break in any competition series we build.
test_idea: For orders under single-award IDVs, compare order extent_competed with the parent IDV value before and after October 2018 and report the mismatch rate by quarter.

claim: DHS contracting staff picked wrong funding office codes in FPDS-NG. DHS said GSA, which runs the Federal Hierarchy feeding FPDS-NG, wrongly added hundreds of offices to the DHS hierarchy.
numbers: Hundreds of offices added. No error rate in the quoted passage.
quote: incorrectly added hundreds of offices to DHS' hierarchy and did not process DHS change requests to inactivate certain offices.
our_interpretation: Office-level errors sit below the awarding agency code we use for cells, so they should not move dollars between our agency cells.
test_idea: Within DHS rows, check that each awarding_office_code maps to one awarding_agency_code across FY2008 to FY2025.

claim: USAspending names FPDS as the authoritative source when procurement data disagree, and points users to the OMB Federal Government Procurement Data Quality Summary.
numbers: none
pinpoint: usaspending.gov/about, Data Quality section, paragraph after "Data Validation"
quote: If there are any discrepancies in procurement data, FPDS is the authoritative source.
our_interpretation: Any USAspending to FPDS mismatch should be resolved in favor of FPDS, which our archive copy cannot do on its own.

claim: USAspending fixed a bug in March 2022 that had shown several awards for one award ID in Advanced Search. It said transactions were unaffected.
numbers: none
pinpoint: Release notes, March 22nd, 2022, Bug Fixes, "Duplicate Awards"
quote: This issue impacted awards only – not transactions.
our_interpretation: Our data are transactions, so this award-level duplication should not double count dollars.

claim: GSA's FPDS help page on reportable actions still shows the 2008 version of FAR 4.606, with interagency agreements and resale on the optional list. The current FAR bars them.
period_covered: Page undated. Text matches the 2008 to 2012 rule.
quote: Interagency agreements, also known as interservice level agreements, memoranda of understanding, or memoranda of agreement.
our_interpretation: Staff guidance that lags the FAR can lead to uneven reporting of these categories after 2012.

claim: Executive Order 14240 of March 20, 2025 directs agencies to have GSA buy common goods and services. It also makes the GSA Administrator executive agent for all government-wide IT acquisition contracts.
numbers: About $490 billion per year spent on common goods and services. Agency proposals due in 60 days, GSA plan in 90 days.
quote: The Federal Government spends approximately $490 billion per year on Federal contracts for common goods and services
our_interpretation: Buying moved to GSA shows up under GSA as awarding agency, so agency cells shrink and GSA cells grow from FY2025 on without any change in demand.
test_idea: awarding_agency_code, funding_agency_code. Share of dollars where awarding agency is 047 and funding agency differs, by FY for FY2022 to FY2025.

claim: OMB reports that in FY2024 $78.2 billion went through GSA vehicles and $16.3 billion was awarded by GSA on behalf of funding agencies as assisted acquisitions. OMB M-25-31 tells agencies to centralize more buying in GSA.
numbers: FY2024 $78.2 billion through GSA vehicles. $16.3 billion GSA-awarded assisted acquisitions. Less than 20 percent of common spend went through GSA. FY2024 common spend $488.9 billion.
quote: In FY 2024, $78.2B went through GSA vehicles and $16.3B was awarded by GSA on behalf of the funding agency (i.e., an “assisted acquisition”).
our_interpretation: Assisted acquisitions put the dollars under GSA as awarding agency, so cells keyed on awarding agency undercount the funding agency.
test_idea: awarding_agency_code 047, funding_agency_code. Net dollars by funding agency for GSA-awarded rows, FY2024 against $16.3 billion.

claim: GSA created an Office of Centralized Acquisition Services to take over procurement authority for designated contracts from other agencies.
quote: OCAS supports agencies as they transition their procurement authority for designated contracts to us.
our_interpretation: Transferred contracts change awarding agency mid-life, so the same award can sit in two agency cells across years.
test_idea: award_id_piid, awarding_agency_code. Count awards whose awarding agency changes between transactions, by FY.

claim: State officials told GAO that several thousand USAID contracts were never updated in FPDS to show the termination, because of the USAID reduction in force.
numbers: Several thousand USAID contracts. GAO matched 1,864 of 3,506 USAID contracts on the DOGE list to FPDS.
quote: there were several thousand contracts that were never updated in FPDS to report them as terminated
our_interpretation: USAID FY2025 cells likely miss termination deobligations, so USAID net dollars are overstated and any later cleanup will land in a later fiscal year.
test_idea: awarding_agency_code 072. Share of FY2025 USAID rows with action_type_code E, F or X against DHS, VA and USDA.

claim: GAO reports that SAM.gov replaced FPDS as the government repository for procurement data on February 24, 2026.
numbers: February 24, 2026.
pinpoint: How GAO Did This Study, footnote 28, p. 11 (PDF p. 11)
quote: on February 24, 2026, SAM.gov replaced the Federal Procurement Data System (FPDS) as the government’s repository for federal procurement information.
our_interpretation: Our 2026-09-06 release was built after this switch, so FY2008 to FY2025 rows now come from the SAM.gov copy of the FPDS database.
test_idea: Row counts and net dollars by FY in this release against an archive pulled before February 24, 2026, if one exists.

claim: SAM.gov states that all FPDS.gov contract award data is now in SAM.gov and that ezSearch was decommissioned on February 24, 2026. Agencies now report through the SAM Contract Awards Management portal, the former FPDS database. The ATOM feed is being replaced by a SAM.gov Contract Awards API that adds deleted contracts.
numbers: New API adds deleted contracts.
pinpoint: Legacy Website and Atom Feed sections
quote: All contract award data that was previously available in FPDS.gov is now available in SAM.gov.
our_interpretation: Deleted records exposed by the new API could later appear or disappear in USAspending releases and shift historical cell totals.

claim: GSA retired FPDS.gov ezSearch on February 24, 2026 and moved all public FPDS functions into SAM.gov. Agency contract writing systems keep reporting through the SAM Contract Awards Management portal, which GSA calls the former FPDS database.
numbers: ezSearch decommissioned February 24, 2026
quote: Agencies’ Contract Writing Systems (CWS) will continue to provide data through the SAM Contract Awards Management web portal (Former FPDS database).
our_interpretation: The data source behind File D1 is the same database under a new front end, so FY2008 to FY2025 rows should be unaffected.

claim: CRS now says SAM.gov is the source of contract award data in USAspending, and that contract award data previously came from FPDS.
quote: Contract award data previously originated from the Federal Procurement Data System.
our_interpretation: The 2026 archive may come from a new pipeline, which should be checked against earlier releases for FY2025.
test_idea: Columns contract_transaction_unique_key, fiscal_year, federal_action_obligation. Compare FY2024 totals in the 2026-09-06 release with an earlier release.

claim: The Broker release of September 22, 2026 mentions an upcoming SAM Contract loader. This points to a new contract data feed into the Broker.
numbers: none
quote: Improved the performance of validations and the upcoming SAM Contract loader.
our_interpretation: A new loader could change how File D1 rows are built in releases after 2026-09-06, so reruns should compare row counts against our release.

claim: GSA says the FPDS ATOM feed will be retired later in FY2026 and replaced by the SAM.gov Contract Awards API.
numbers: none
quote: The FPDS.gov ATOM Feed will be retired later in FY 2026.
our_interpretation: USAspending has loaded contract data from the FPDS feed, so a feed change in FY2026 is a point to watch for future archive releases.

claim: FPDS records a termination but does not say whether it was complete or partial. GAO adds that an undetermined part of the terminated contracts is still active.
quote: FPDS data do not distinguish between complete and partial terminations.
our_interpretation: A termination modification in our data tells us a contract was cut but not by how much, so only the dollar amount on the row shows the size of the cut.
test_idea: action_type_code E, F, X. Count FY2025 termination rows with later positive obligations on the same award.

claim: USDA contracting systems code every termination for convenience as one value that covers complete and partial terminations. The systems cannot tell the two apart.
pinpoint: Footnote 2, p. 1 (PDF p. 5), repeated in footnote 7, p. 3 (PDF p. 7)
quote: The systems do not differentiate between full or partial terminations.
our_interpretation: This matches GAO and means termination rows cannot be used to mark an award as ended.

claim: USDA terminated 792 contracts for convenience in FY2025. Net deobligations reached $64.4 million by March 20, 2026, and vendors have up to one year to file settlement proposals.
numbers: 792 contracts. $558.3 million obligated. $64.4 million net deobligations. At least $4.9 million settlement costs. Closeout takes 6 to 36 months. Last FY2025 termination September 25, 2025.
quote: Vendors have up to 1 year post termination to submit a settlement proposal. As such, the total financial impact of the termination actions may change as the contracts proceed through the settlement and contract closeout processes
our_interpretation: Deobligations from FY2025 terminations keep arriving in FY2026 and later, so FY2025 vendor totals may look higher than the final cost of those contracts.
test_idea: awarding_agency_code 012, action_type_code F. Sum federal_action_obligation on termination rows by FY.

claim: Savings figures for terminated contracts ignore later obligations and deobligations from settlement costs and closeout. GAO concludes the reported savings are likely misstated.
quote: terminated contracts do not account for subsequent obligations and deobligations that may be associated with termination settlement costs or contract close out. As such, the amount of reported savings is likely misstated.
our_interpretation: Dollars tied to FY2025 terminations keep moving in FY2026 and later, so FY2025 cells in later releases will not change but the related flows will land in later fiscal years.

claim: DHS met the needs of 30 terminated IT IDIQ contracts through existing government-wide contracts. It obligated over $1.7 billion that way in FY2025.
numbers: 30 IDIQ contracts carried about $10 billion (95%) of the $10.5 billion claimed cost avoidance. Over $1.7 billion obligated in FY2025 through government-wide contracts.
quote: in fiscal year 2025, DHS obligated over $1.7 billion through existing government-wide contracts to meet these requirements.
our_interpretation: Dollars in DHS IT cells shift in FY2025 from the terminated IDIQ holders to vendors on government-wide vehicles, which changes shares without a change in demand.
test_idea: awarding_agency_code 070, product_or_service_code D and 7 families, parent_award_id_piid. Vendor shares in FY2024 and FY2025.

claim: DoD File C to File D1 linkage fell sharply in FY2024 and FY2025. Linked DoD procurement awards were 944,252 in FY2019 P12 and 554,163 in FY2023 P12, then 137,180 in FY2024 P12, 28,962 in FY2025 P6 and 25,729 in FY2025 P12. Unlinked FPDS awards rose from 50,295 to 436,136.
pinpoint: response keys unlinked_file_d_award_count, total_linked_award_count (FY2024 P12). Other years in sources USAS-UNLINKED-097-FY2018-P12 to USAS-UNLINKED-097-FY2025-P12
quote: {"unlinked_file_c_award_count":2,"unlinked_file_d_award_count":401922,"total_linked_award_count":137180}
our_interpretation: The collapse sits in DoD account data and leaves the FPDS side intact, but it means most DoD contract awards with FY2024 and FY2025 activity lack treasury account and DEFC detail on USAspending.

claim: GSA put its work on plans to modernize FPDS and the other remaining legacy systems on hold by May 2025. OMB had not issued its procurement data quality summary for FY2023 or FY2024 by May 5, 2025.
numbers: Plans on hold May 2025. No OMB summary for FY2023 or FY2024 as of May 5, 2025.
pinpoint: p. 32 (PDF p. 37), footnote 47 on p. 25 (PDF p. 30)
quote: Additionally, in May 2025, PMO officials told us that their efforts to develop plans were on hold.
our_interpretation: No official accuracy summary exists for FY2023 or FY2024, so our most recent years lack even the government's self-reported quality figures.

claim: The fall 2025 lapse in appropriations lasted 42 days, from October 1 through November 11, 2025. P.L. 119-37, signed November 12, 2025, ended it.
numbers: 42-day lapse. October 1, 2025 to November 11, 2025. P.L. 119-37 enacted November 12, 2025.
quote: The enactment of P.L. 119-37 ended a 42-day lapse in appropriations (a “funding gap”) lasting from October 1, 2025, through November 11, 2025.
our_interpretation: The lapse falls after FY2025 ended, so it can only delay late FY2025 entries and corrections, including DoD rows held for 90 days.
test_idea: action_date in FY2025 Q4 and last_modified_date. Count FY2025 rows first loaded during October 1 to November 11, 2025 against the same window in 2024.

claim: The GSA lapse plan says activities of the Federal Acquisition Service that are funded through the Acquisition Services Fund are exempt from the lapse. The plan does not name FPDS, SAM.gov or the Integrated Award Environment.
numbers: 3,496 GSA employees retained because funded outside annual appropriations (2,687 under the ASF).
pinpoint: Para. 4.o(1), Federal Acquisition Service, p. 17 (PDF p. 17)
quote: FAS activities that are funded through the ASF are exempt as the ASF is a revolving fund that is not immediately affected by a lapse in appropriations.
our_interpretation: We found no government document saying FPDS or USAspending stopped updating during the lapse.

claim: GAO reports federal contract obligations of $792.77 billion in FY2025 and $756.18 billion in FY2024, from USAspending data as of April 2026.
numbers: FY2024 $756.18 billion. FY2025 $792.77 billion.
quote: Source: GAO analysis of USAspending.gov data as of April 2026
our_interpretation: These totals give an outside check on our FY2024 and FY2025 net dollars, allowing for differences in scope.
test_idea: Sum of federal_action_obligation for FY2024 and FY2025 against $756.18 billion and $792.77 billion.

claim: DOGE listed 13,476 contracts as terminated, but FPDS shows no termination action on 2,503 of them. Those 2,503 carry $27.4 billion of the claimed savings.
numbers: 13,476 contracts listed. 2,503 with no termination action. $27.4 billion of $61.0 billion claimed. 3,751 entries (27.8%) had no contract number.
quote: No termination action was taken on 2,503 of the contracts, representing $27.4 billion of reported savings.
our_interpretation: The DOGE list is not a reliable index of terminations, so we should identify terminations only from FPDS action_type_code.

claim: DHS fully or partially terminated 438 contracts from January 20 through September 30, 2025. DHS had obligated over $1.6 billion on them before termination and deobligated a net $92 million since.
numbers: 438 contracts. $1,670,143,632 obligated before termination. Net deobligation over $92 million through March 31, 2026. DHS FY2025 contract obligations about $28.4 billion.
quote: DHS fully or partially terminated 438 contracts from January 20 through September 30, 2025. Over $1.6 billion had been obligated on these contracts prior to their termination.
our_interpretation: Net termination deobligations at DHS are about 0.3% of its FY2025 contract obligations, so they move few cells much.
test_idea: awarding_agency_code 070, action_type_code F, FY2025. Count distinct awards and sum federal_action_obligation, compare with 438 and $92 million.

claim: VA terminated 435 contract actions for convenience in 2025, valued at about $1.1 billion, out of 2,210 actions the OIG reviewed. Lists VA sent to Congress were wrong, and some actions were terminated and then reinstated.
numbers: 435 terminated of 2,210 reviewed. About $1.1 billion. 11 actions terminated then reinstated on the May 2025 list. VA FY2025 contract obligations $78.3 billion.
quote: The OIG determined that VA terminated 435 contracts for convenience
our_interpretation: VA terminations are small next to $78.3 billion in obligations, but reinstated actions can leave a termination row followed by new obligations on the same award.
test_idea: awarding_agency_code 036, action_type_code F, FY2025. Count awards with a termination row followed by a positive obligation.

claim: GAO notes the FAR is being rewritten under the Revolutionary FAR Overhaul (Executive Order 14275, April 2025). GAO cites the pre-overhaul FAR (legacy) for FY2025 actions.
numbers: Executive Order 14275 of April 2025.
quote: The FAR (legacy) is referenced in this report since this review focuses on fiscal year 2025.
our_interpretation: FY2025 rows were reported under the legacy rules, but any change to FPDS reporting rules under the overhaul would affect FY2026 and later releases.

claim: Under the Revolutionary FAR Overhaul, FAR subpart 4.6 becomes section 4.301. Optional reporting now needs written approval from OFPP, and the annual certification goes to OFPP within 120 days.
numbers: 120 days.
period_covered: Model deviation 2025, adopted by agency class deviations from about August 2025
agencies: Agencies adopting the RFO Part 4 deviation
quote: Agencies may submit actions other than those listed at paragraph (a)(1) of this section if approved in writing by the Office of Federal Procurement Policy (OFPP).
our_interpretation: The exclusion list is unchanged, so coverage in FY2025 should match earlier years, but the approval route for optional rows changed.

claim: The RFO text keeps all eleven exclusions from FAR 4.606(c), including classified actions and interagency agreements, and raises the generic identifier limit for individuals abroad to $40,000.
agencies: Agencies adopting the RFO Part 4 deviation
quote: Contract actions in which the required data would constitute classified information.
our_interpretation: The scope of our data does not change under the RFO.

claim: GSA adopted the FAR Council's Part 4 model deviation on August 13, 2025. The memo says section 4.301 consolidates and streamlines the reporting rules of subpart 4.6.
quote: consolidates and streamlines the reporting requirements from subpart 4.6.
our_interpretation: Different agencies switched to the RFO text on different dates in late FY2025, which is a paperwork change for our scope.

claim: GAO matched FY2023 to FY2024 USAspending.gov awards to SAM by UEI. Of 20.3 million contract and assistance awards, 12.8 million had a valid UEI, 7.4 million had none (mostly aggregate assistance awards) and 2,969 had a UEI that did not match SAM.
numbers: 20.3 million awards. 12.8 million valid UEI. 7.4 million without UEI. 2,969 invalid UEI. Downloaded February 3, 2025 (Table 10).
quote: We were able to link most of the fiscal years 2023 and 2024 USAspending.gov award data to SAM entity information using UEIs.
our_interpretation: Invalid recipient UEIs are very rare, and the awards without a UEI are mostly aggregate grants, so recipient UEI coverage on recent contract rows looks good.
test_idea: recipient_uei, action_date_fiscal_year: share of FY2023 to FY2025 contract rows and dollars with blank or malformed recipient UEI.

claim: GSA notes that NASA award data may be obtained from the SAM Data Bank, apart from the general contract award search.
numbers: none
quote: NASA Award data may be obtained from the SAM Data Bank
our_interpretation: NASA keeps agency-specific FPDS elements, and the page does not say whether NASA records are complete in the new search.

claim: FAR 4.606(a)(1) requires agencies to report any modification that changes previously reported contract action data, regardless of dollar value. Termination modifications therefore must be reported to FPDS.
quote: agencies must report any modification to these contract actions that change previously reported contract action data, regardless of dollar value
our_interpretation: Termination modifications are in our transaction data, so their deobligations already reduce vendor net totals.
test_idea: action_type_code, federal_action_obligation. Count and sum rows with codes E, F, N and X by FY.

claim: DoD guidance requires a modification report for any obligation or deobligation and a minus sign for a net deobligation. Terminations for default or cause must also be reported to FAPIIS.
quote: When entering a net deobligation on a contract action, include the minus (-) sign.
our_interpretation: Termination deobligations appear as negative federal_action_obligation, which explains some negative vendor totals in our findings.
test_idea: federal_action_obligation less than 0 and action_type_code E, F or X. Share of negative dollars from terminations by FY.

claim: The FPDS data element Reason for Modification, published by USAspending as action_type, has separate codes for terminations. E is terminate for default, F is terminate for convenience, X is terminate for cause and N is legal contract cancellation.
numbers: Codes E, F, N, X.
quote: F = TERMINATE FOR CONVENIENCE (COMPLETE OR PARTIAL)
our_interpretation: We can isolate termination rows by action_type_code, which lets us measure how much FY2025 dollars changed through terminations.
test_idea: action_type_code in E, F, N, X. Net dollars by awarding agency for FY2015 to FY2025, FY2025 against the prior ten-year mean.
